#8668. The Ultimate Life Coach

Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.

You’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises. And then to put thousands of hours into everything else I value as well: family, health, friends, adventures, building stuff, and even writing the occasional blog post. No complaints about any of this.

But if I can indulge you to play me a brief Tiny Violin of First World Problems solo, even this perfect life comes with one flaw: I never have to do anything I don’t want to do.

To most people, this sounds like a dream come true. Especially if you combine total freedom with plenty of money, life is just a non-stop blissful playground of self actualization, right?

Well, maybe, but maybe not. In reality, the answer depends on who you are.

Freedom and money reveal a person’s true strengths and weaknesses, and the result is a spectrum with “Unlimited drugs and booze on the couch” at one end, and “Create and manage a series of nonprofit foundations which employ thousands of people to research and invest in medical advances and clean energy” at the other.

For most of my journey so far, I seem to have found the balance pretty naturally. My Dad job was very intense for the first decade, but somehow I also had time to build and restore quite a few houses in the neighborhood, take plenty of intense trips to interesting places, give some talks and make some videos, and still write a few hundred blog posts.

But in these last few years, I have started slowing down, and it has become more and more difficult to wrangle and focus myself to get these things to happen as often.

Instead of constantly bouncing around the construction site building cool things, or falling into laser focus on the keyboard finishing an article that I just had to share with you, I found myself retiring to the couch earlier and earlier each afternoon, seeking distraction on the phone and wishing I had the energy and focus to do those other more enjoyable things.

So I fought back, by learning more about health and wellness. Trying to study and train my way into more energy and focus and motivation. And you’ve seen some of the results here, in articles I’ve shared about daily habits, steering clear of excessive comfort, and more.

And all of these things really work, IF you take the knowledge and actually put it into action. And therein lies the problem:

I kept learning effective new things, and successfully incorporating them into my life. They would work for a while, but gradually my brain would invent various excuses to stop doing them consistently, leaving me with plenty of knowledge but far too little accomplishment to show for it.

Until finally, just a few months ago, I realized that I had been sabotaging my own progress by turning my biggest life advantage into a disadvantage:

I have been using my freedom too much – in order to avoid doing things that I didn’t feel like doing.

See, freedom is great if it frees you from leaving your children at 5am so you can drive an hour through a traffic jam to sit in an office building for nine hours. But that same freedom goes to waste if you then just plunk the kids down in front of a playlist of cheap cartoons while you lounge in the corner to scroll Facebook all day.

You need to use it to do things that are even more valuable than the job you just quit. And if you can’t do that, you might as well just keep the damned job.

This is what I was doing, while lying about it to myself. I would focus on the easy things which are still good for me, like taking care of the house or hanging out with friends who live nearby. But I avoid doing the harder things – which for me means the things that require more planning, energy or focus. Even though these are the things that allow me to lead the life I enjoy most.

Let’s use workouts as an easy example. I already know that on a minute-for-minute basis, this is the single most effective thing almost anybody can do with their time because it drastically improves every other area of life. But despite knowing this, I was still following this pattern:

“I want to get in a really good weight training workout today.But I don’t feel like doing a workout because it’s hard.So I’ll try to grease the wheels for myself so it’s easier to achieve. I’ll pick the perfect time of day when the weather is nice, and my energy level is high. I’ll set up my gym in advance the night before.And when that golden moment of perfect conditions hits,I’ll hit the gym!“

But between you and me, that moment didn’t always come. Some weeks I’d achieve it 2-3 times, some weeks I’d get “busy” and make excuses like “well at least I walked a lot today”. Some days I would complete a great workout, but when recording it in the journal I’d see that the previous one was over a week ago.

And the results of this lackluster effort were exactly what you’d expect: lackluster fitness.

Then something changed and I learned that there’s a much better way to get those workouts done. It’s by replacing the long, meandering, frankly wussypants dialog above with this one:

I want to work out today.I don’t feel like it.^^^ AHA!! I JUST CAUGHT MYSELF TRYING TO SELF SABOTAGE! ^^^I am now already putting on my shoes and walking to the gym.

I’m using workouts as an example because this is the behavior I managed to change most successfully, but the exact same technique applies to everything else that you or I want to do, but fail to do regularly.

The key is learning to watch over yourself like an Eagle and identify that exact moment of hesitation.

And then instead of using it as a trigger for excuses, you use it as a trigger for action.

It’s so counterintuitive at first, but then obvious in retrospect. Hesitance feels shitty in the moment, and it really can ruin your life if you listen to it too often. But the ultimate solution is usually to run directly towards, rather than away from, the stuff you don’t want to do.

So really, Hesitation can be the ultimate life coach.

As part of writing this article, I shared the idea around with friends to test it out first. And I was initially surprised to get mixed results. About half of them could relate with me: they felt they were underachieving in life and wanted to do more. The other half though I was crazy: these people feel they are already doing too much, raising multiple kids and managing multiple businesses and training for ironman triathlons in the mountains.

The overachievers go through life nicely buzzed but often stressed. When hearing them describe their schedules, I was absolutely not envious. At the same time, they weren’t impressed with my schedule either because it’s too easy. We could both benefit from making adjustments towards the center.

Impressive overachiever friends are one thing, but the thing that really flipped the switch for me was hearing a podcast interview with our planet’s most extreme example of driving yourself beyond your former limits, David Goggins.

I learned about his life story with a mix of awe and horror. Severely beaten as a child, he grew up with a looming wall of psychological demons and issues, but his reaction was the unique part: he has been driven to compulsively seek out and overcome extreme hardship, not just to unimaginable levels but hundreds of times beyond that.

From pushing through several near-death experiences just to qualify for a Navy SEALS career, to breaking his own legs, heart and lungs from the constant exertion of things like running 240 miles over four days without sleeping, to setting a world record of 4025 bar pull ups over 24 hours (shredding his hands to look like ground beef in the process), the man does things I would never have thought are even close to possible for a human.

And that flipped a switch for me, by putting my own incredibly easy, under-achieving life into perspective.

Because while I absolutely do not want any part of the Goggins life, and I would gladly live my life never having run more than 10 miles at a single stretch, I do find it incredibly helpful to learn that pretty much all of our barriers are entirely mental, not physical or placed upon us by the outside world.

Sure, we do have different starting points and different amounts of luck. But instead of thinking of life like this:

I now realize that things are more like this:

And that’s a really empowering way to think about life, that feels like the sky has opened way up.

So the podcast was just an introduction. I wrote down the particularly concise quote “You already fuckin’ know what to do.” on a piece of cardstock, stuck it to my bathroom mirror, and started acting on it immediately.

Suddenly, I was able to hit the gym every single day because I had two ways to approach it: wanting to put in a workout, and not wanting to put in a workout, either of which became a trigger to work out immediately.

And of course, once I finally put in the effort, it started working. Even though I’ve been sorta into this type of training since I was a teenager, I have mostly floated along on a plateau for years. But with this change in attitude, I gained ten pounds of lean weight over the first four months, returning to the strength and flexibility that I had at age 25, and every single joint in my body feels like it has been upgraded to a study, well oiled spring.

I also used the “catch yourself at the moment of hesitance” trick to get myself to run instead of walk more often (over 20 runs since I got back to Colorado last month), get over to the MMM-HQ coworking space for more work and socializing visits, and even to sit back down at the computer to write this post for you. While I’ve found that too much blogger work (and internet “success”) is a bad thing, there is still a right level that works for me. But it takes a lot of discipline to be willing to do it, because of all the other easier and more thrilling activities I could be doing with this same stretch of time.

For me, fully internalizing this one powerful piece of inspiring profanity has been transformative. But I still find that returning regularly to the well makes all this work even better. So I downloaded both of the Goggins audiobooks and worked through them in little chunks on my morning walks over the period of a month. Then I moved on to Peter Attia’s Outlive, and Jocko Willink’s Extreme Ownership.

While the intellectuals fret about the perils of “Bro Science” or the “Toxic Masculinity” of today’s tribe of health podcasters and question their motivation, I simply absorb the messages that work for me and discard the rest. Find people who make you reach a little higher, and feed on their energy.

And for me, being exposed to successful, strong, athletic people who squeeze a lot of work out of themselves is a big source of inspiration. It helps me do more with my day, which is exactly what works for me right now at this phase of life.

And I wish you more of what works for you too!

Started reading your blog in 2018 and it has been a constant source of inspiration and help. I am 32 and left the relatively high paying banking job at 27 to build a start up. And my needs are so low that I don’t have the desire to make loads of money therefore I don’t have the motivation to do the work’.

This, of course, is rubbish. I know deep down we want to be creative, productive and a service to others but it has just been tricky finding the ‘why’ to do it. Your article here will be a great help. It is incredible how timely your articles seem to be in my own life.

Only this week I seem to have overcome the first hurdle a little and have started writing my own newsletter. An interesting stat that I read recently that has really helped with my motivation was this. People that do ‘hard’ things for long-term reasons, i.e. ‘I exercise to live longer’ or ‘I exercise to be healthy’, do 30% less exercise than people who exercise for the immediate benefits like ‘I want to feel better today!’ or ‘I exercise to feel more energised TODAY’.

I gave this reframing a go for sitting down to write. I changed from ‘I want to write so that in the future I will have a newsletter that serves others and makes me money’ to ‘I want to write because of the state of flow I will feel in the moment and the sense of achievement I will feel TODAY’. It has completely energised me and increased my motivation to do the thing I have been putting off because ‘I don’t have to do it’.

I will implement your advice above alongside this reframing and hopefully soon you will be reading my newsletter in the same way I have read yours over the years :).

Some things that make me feel healthy, happy, and strong that I know I should do more of: weight training, mountain biking, backpacking in the mountains, keeping my house and garage workshop clean and organized, designing and building things, helping other people with home projects, cooking.

One thing I do that helps me stay focused on these things is turn off ALL notifications on my phone, then selectively turn on the few notifications I actually want to know about. I only get notified for text messages, voice mails, calendar reminders, and a few other things. There are often days when I get zero notifications on my phone.

This may not be for everyone, but I also don’t use any social media or read/watch hardly any news. I do watch youtube, but no facebook, instagram, twitter, tik tok, etc. For me all of these things feel like they are vying to “steal” my focus and make it harder to have a calm mind and energy to focus on the things I know I should be doing. I want to work out today. I don’t feel like it. ^^^ AHA!! I JUST CAUGHT MYSELF TRYING TO SELF SABOTAGE! ^^^ I am now already putting on my shoes and walking to the gym.

. . . is pure Stoicism, a topic you have touched on before.

That little voice in your head that says “I don’t feel like it” is what the Stoics called “an impression.” You have clearly learned to apply “prosoche” (mindfulness would be a good translation of this Greek word) to interrogate that impression. Then you applied natural wisdom (one of the Stoic virtues) to reach the logical conclusion that surrendering to that impression would not be in your best interest.

There is another Stoic echo in your rediscovered commitment to exercise. The Stoics strongly believed that it was crucial to constantly test oneself, whether that meant fasting, walking barefoot in the now, or undertaking difficult or unpleasant tasks.

So well done! You are proving an apt “prokopton” (one who is making progress to becoming a Stoic sage).

As a retired person I can really relate to this. For me it’s not the lack of desire to do hard things, it’s the easy distracting nature of the phone. I get bored, pull out my phone, then wonder where the last eight hours went.

People with jobs and young kids have to put down the phone to go to work, or take the kids to school. I could spend 100% of my time on YouTube, and my brain will do that if I let it.

My retired quality of life improved immensely when I started keeping my phone and computer in my office out of reach.

Now I get bored, feel uncomfortable, then go and do something. That feeling of boredom and discomfort is critical to making me do the things that actually bring joy to my life.

Boredom is a signal that I have spare energy that should be used for something. Phones alleviate boredom and kill motivation

Little off topic, but what were your final thoughts of Culdesac in Arizona? Would you ever consider moving there? Was there a sense of community and collaboration?

Hey RH, thanks for following along with that. Throughout my stay there, I kept this page updated, and it’s now in its final form with all my thoughts so far: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/

Summary: there is *some* community forming there, but not as much as I expected going in – they’re still working on building out the neighborhood so it’s a tough chicken-and-egg problem to crack. How do you attract people who really want to hang out with their neighbors rather than just people looking to hide away in their apartments? The Culdesac team are fantastic however, and of course the physical architecture of the place is beautiful. So I think they are doing the right things to build it out.

Glad to hear you’re picking up Extreme Ownership! As someone who is still in his working years, it’s made the way I think about getting work done much better. In software engineering, sometimes shit just goes wrong. Knowing that almost everything can be avoided by us engineers doing a better and robust job has improved the way I work and has made me _less_ stressed, because the work I do is better and more well thought out from the start. Even when something does go wrong, it’s just a learning experience that allows me to avoid those pitfalls in the future.

This book is even better for your social relationships though! Most of the time, you can be the ignition to a better relationship with someone. I’ve seen it many times where relationships you want drift away because neither side initiates social interaction enough with the other. “If they really care, they’d reach out.” Turns out, if you take ownership and reach out, you’ll see them a lot more and be happier as a result. The same thing applies for someone toxic in your life. Tired of this person bringing you down? Take ownership and remove yourself from the equation. (Obviously there are circumstances where this doesn’t apply, but you’ll know it when you see it).

Plus the narration of the audiobook is just great. Jocko has that Seal Team motivational way of speaking that makes you get your shit together!

Thank you for posting this and articulating ideas many are feeling on this blog. I have found a social approach works best for keeping me motivated to work out. My partner is training for a canoe trip in Canada, so we both ride our bikes to the gym twice a week. On both days I go to a weight training class for older adults. I like the work out, the instructors and my classmates. Oh yeah, and they play Beatles music.

I also get yearly DXA scans. Last year my scans were horrible and that motivated me to start regular strength training. This year I have improved and that motivates me to keep working out.

Not everything is mental unfortunately. I have all kinds of motivation and willingness to push myself, but no matter what I do, my body is just not in the condition that it was 10 – 15 years ago, and the aches and pains that result from pushing myself prevent me from doing anything more than walking at this point in my life. So, this advice is great if you don’t have any medical conditions preventing you from pushing yourself, however, I believe that there are many people out there like myself who are not built like Goggins.

I realise you have said you don’t swallow the whole Goggins creed, Mr. Moustache, but Goggins? In any measure? Really?

I am surprised you haven’t learnt by now that always pushing your limits, redlining your body, is not a formula for health, fitness and well-being; it is the road to injury and burnout.

There are countless examples of exercise fanatics who started off thinking, with Nietzsche, that ‘That which doesn’t kill me makes me stronger’. They end up realising that ‘That which doesn’t kill me can still cripple me’.

Just look at poor old Ronnie Coleman. https://youtu.be/kq0Sm4kAp4Y?si=_ma2zjT_WoWVi4wC

But after many injuries, all self-inflicted and therefore avoidable, I have developed a different philosophy: Progress over perfection; You won’t improve from something you can’t recover from; Little by little, step by step, work on your weaknesses and limitations; No brain, no gain.

Could your procrastination stem from thinking that exercise is a gruelling, penitential task? Why not just resolve to show up everyday and just do something — some mobility work, an easy jog, a few sets of easy pull-ups and hanging leg raises? Some days that will put you in the mood to push harder, go further— fine. Other days you can stop there — also fine. Just keep showing up and making deposits into the Bank (or ETF, or whatever) of Fitness. They will add up, and sometimes compound, just like money. Health and fitness is a long game, just like saving and investment.

There is definitely a time and place to test your mettle — generally in a competition or emergency. But suffering is not how you get fitter. ‘The ability to suffer during a workout is just one skill. Don’t over-focus on it. You also need to train a hundred other skills’.https://youtu.be/0h23IANIg6Q For most workouts, the goal should be to finish feeling better than when you started. Energised, not exhausted. If tired, sore, and injured are the side-effects, is it worth it?

Of course, who am I to say what will motivate you? But I know that when I changed my outlook from struggle-&-suffer to small, manageable steps, every day my hesitation vanished and I became keen to show up.

Exactly, I think we’re saying the same thing here. If you read the article, you’ll notice I have no interest in any of the Goggins-style self flogging. It says right in there “reasonable effort”, and I also mentioned that I don’t even need to run ten miles at a time. I’m well aware that overdoing it in any one physical activity leads to injury!

And an interesting side note: doing a healthy amount of strength (weight) training has the opposite effect – it serves as the ultimate injury preventer. I first took up the practice at age 14, making do with those flimsy plastic hand-me-down barbell plates in my tiny bedroom at home. And since then I’ve never had a real physical injury, my knees and back have been miraculously perfect despite all sorts of skiing, snowboarding, mountain biking, moving around wheelbarrows of concrete and carrying washing machines and pianos up and down staircases. My body is a piece of work equipment and I really want it to keep working hard for me for decades to come!

So anyway, I’m only using the Goggins mentality to catch myself when I want to skip out on a difficult thing – whether it’s showing up for what might be an easy workout, or making the phone call to the repair company to get my windshield fixed. Small manageable steps, but I have to DO them.

The highest-value hotel redemption for families using Chase Ultimate Rewards

Picture this: your kids are splashing in an infinity pool that overlooks the turquoise Caribbean, your partner is sipping a cocktail at the swim-up bar, and you're on your third gourmet meal of the day — all without opening your wallet once. No mental math at dinner. No "should we do the excursion?" budget anxiety. Just a genuinely luxurious family vacation where everything is already paid for. This is what the Hyatt All-Inclusive sweet spot feels like. And the ChooseFI community has quietly been using it to take family vacations that their neighbors are financing on credit card debt — except you're doing it nearly free. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva property — think Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, or Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana — will typically run **$500 to $1,500 per night** in cash when you factor in the all-inclusive rate for two adults and two kids. Over a five-night stay, you're looking at a cash outlay of $2,500 to $7,500. That's a trip many families save years for. With World of Hyatt points, that same night costs **25,000 points**. At a cash rate of $1,000 per night (a very achievable number at peak Ziva properties), you're extracting **4 cents per point** in value — and at $1,500 per night, you're pushing **6 cents per point**. The industry benchmark for a "good" hotel redemption is 1-2 cents per point. You're doubling or tripling that benchmark on a family vacation. The pricing inefficiency here is structural and beautiful: Hyatt's award chart is **fixed**, meaning they set a category for each property based on its tier, not its cash price. All-inclusive resorts are priced in the award chart like any other Hyatt — but the cash rate includes *every meal, every drink, every activity*. The loyalty program hasn't fully "priced in" the all-inclusive premium. That gap is your opportunity. For families pursuing FI, this redemption is especially powerful because the value scales with family size. Four people eating and drinking all day at a resort adds up fast in cash — but costs exactly the same 25,000 points whether it's two people or a family of six. The bigger your family, the more you win.

The core insight here is understanding what the 25,000 points actually buys — and why Hyatt's award chart creates an accidental arbitrage for all-inclusive resorts.

World of Hyatt uses a fixed award chart, categorizing properties from Category 1 (3,500 points/night) to Category 8 (45,000 points/night). Hyatt Ziva and Hyatt Zilara properties typically fall in the Category 4–6 range (18,000–25,000 points/night depending on the specific property and season). The key word is fixed: your points cost doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash prices do. A sold-out week during spring break or Christmas holiday that drives cash rates to $1,500/night still costs the same 25,000 points as an off-peak Tuesday.

Now layer on the all-inclusive structure. When you book a Hyatt Ziva or Hyatt Zilara on points, all meals, drinks, and activities are included in the award rate. This isn't a separate fee. This isn't a resort charge tacked on. The award redemption covers the full all-inclusive experience — the same unlimited dining, premium open bar, water sports, and entertainment that cash guests pay for. Hyatt is one of the few hotel brands that doesn't strip out the all-inclusive component when you book with points.

The Transfer Path: Chase Ultimate Rewards to World of Hyatt

This is where the ChooseFI earning strategy snaps into place. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, instantly. There's no waiting period, no processing delay — you initiate the transfer and the points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, instantly, which matters if you're earning points on rent payments through the Bilt Mastercard.

The transfer ratio is significant because Chase UR points are among the easiest transferable points to earn in volume. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Chase Ink Business Preferred, and Chase Ink Business Cash/Unlimited (when paired with a Sapphire card) all feed into the same UR pool. A family spending across categories can accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually, which translates directly into four or more nights at a Ziva property.

World of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges or carrier-imposed fees on award bookings. The only cost you'll pay out-of-pocket is the government taxes on your award night — typically $10–25 per night depending on the property location. Your 25,000 points buys you a clean, nearly free night without surprise fees draining the value.

Family vs. Adults-Only: Know Which Property to Book

Hyatt Ziva properties are family-friendly — kids are welcome, family suites are available, and there are dedicated kids' clubs and activities. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only. This distinction matters enormously when booking. Searching for availability and finding great dates at a Zilara won't help if you're bringing a 9-year-old. Always confirm the property type before transferring points.

Before searching for availability, confirm your points position. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account at chase.com/ultimaterewards and check your combined UR balance across all eligible cards. Remember, points from Chase Ink cards can be pooled with your Sapphire Reserve or Preferred. You'll need at least 25,000 points per night you want to book — a five-night trip requires 125,000 points. If you're close but not there, set a target date 3–4 months out and focus earning in the meantime.

Go to hyatt.com and search for your target property directly. Use the "Use Points" toggle to see award availability. Key properties to search for families:

For adults-only trips, search Hyatt Zilara Cancun or Hyatt Zilara Cap Cana. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, so you can search nearly 13 months ahead — this is your best window for securing prime dates like school breaks, spring break, and holiday weeks.

Search flexible date ranges to find the best combination of availability and value. Hyatt's calendar view makes this efficient — you can see which nights have standard award availability vs. premium pricing. Note that some peak dates may show higher point requirements; always check if your target dates are at the standard 25,000-point rate or a peak rate.

Once you've confirmed award availability for your exact dates, navigate to Chase Ultimate Rewards and select "Transfer to Travel Partners." Choose World of Hyatt from the partner list. The transfer ratio is 1:1 and the transfer is instant — your Hyatt points will appear within minutes. Only transfer what you need for the specific booking; there's no reason to transfer excess points speculatively.

Return to hyatt.com, log into your World of Hyatt account, and complete the award booking for your confirmed dates. At checkout, select points as your payment method. You'll pay only minimal government taxes (typically $10–25/night). Keep your confirmation email — it will specify that the all-inclusive meals, beverages, and activities are included.

Award availability at popular Ziva/Zilara properties can be limited during peak school break windows. Your moves: (1) Search 395 days out as soon as your target dates open, (2) consider shoulder season dates that offer strong weather but lower demand, (3) call the World of Hyatt member line at 1-800-323-7249 — agents sometimes see availability the website doesn't display, (4) check alternate Ziva/Zilara properties in different destinations.

The math on Hyatt all-inclusive redemptions is what makes this a true sweet spot for the FI community. At a standard hotel, your points cover the room — but you still pay cash for meals, drinks, and activities. At an all-inclusive, the points rate covers everything: room, all meals, unlimited drinks, pool and beach access, kids clubs, entertainment, and most resort activities. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva paying $700 per night in cash (a common rate) would spend $4,900 for a 7-night stay — plus tips. The same stay at 25,000 points per night costs 175,000 World of Hyatt points total, which equals approximately $3,500 in transferable points value at a conservative 2 cents per point. But the actual value received is closer to $5,000 to $7,000 when you factor in all the meals, drinks, and activities that would cost extra at a regular hotel. This is why Hyatt all-inclusives consistently deliver 3 to 4 cents per point — double the already-strong Hyatt average.

Let's walk through a real family booking so you can see exactly how the numbers work.

The Trip: 5 Nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun for a Family of Four

You're planning a spring break trip — mid-April, when the weather in Cancun is spectacular and school is out. A family of four (two adults, two kids) wants five nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, one of the flagship all-inclusive properties in Hyatt's portfolio. This is a beachfront resort with multiple restaurants, a waterpark-style pool complex, and dedicated kids' programming.

The Cash Price: During spring break, Hyatt Ziva Cancun's all-inclusive rate for a family room runs approximately $900–$1,200 per night for a standard room, all meals and drinks included. At $1,000/night average, five nights costs $5,000 cash. At $1,200/night, you're at $6,000. That's real money for a family.

The Points Cost: At 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night, five nights costs 125,000 points. You'll pay approximately $75–100 total in government taxes across the stay. That's it.

The CPP Math: $5,000 value ÷ 125,000 points = 4 cents per point. At the higher cash rate of $6,000, you're at 4.8 cents per point. The World of Hyatt program's own editorial value benchmark is considered strong at 1.7 cents per point — you're earning nearly 3x that benchmark on this booking.

What Your Family Actually Gets: Every breakfast, lunch, and dinner at the resort's full-service restaurants. Unlimited alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages from morning coffee to late-night cocktails. The resort's pool complex with water slides the kids will talk about for years. Non-motorized water sports. Evening entertainment. This isn't a stripped-down experience — Hyatt Ziva is an upper-upscale brand, and the quality of food and service reflects it.

The Transfer: You move 125,000 Chase UR points to World of Hyatt at 1:1 — instantly — and book directly on hyatt.com. The entire booking process takes under 30 minutes once you have availability confirmed.

Book at the 395-Day Window for Peak Dates

Hyatt opens its booking window 395 days in advance — that's about 13 months. For spring break, Christmas week, and Thanksgiving, set a calendar reminder and search the moment your target dates become available. Families who wait until 6 months out regularly find those prime weeks already gone on points. This is the single biggest mistake families make with this redemption.

Search Multiple Properties to Triangulate Availability

Don't anchor on one property. Run searches simultaneously at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, and Hyatt Ziva Rose Hall. Different properties have different award release patterns, and finding five consecutive nights at one property is easier than it sounds if you're flexible about which destination.

Use 5th Night Free to Stretch Your Points Further

World of Hyatt has a 5th night free on award stays benefit for World of Hyatt credit card holders. Book five nights and pay points for only four. On a 5-night Ziva trip, that saves 25,000 points — enough for one additional night. If you have or are considering the World of Hyatt Credit Card, this benefit alone justifies it for this specific redemption.

The fastest path to 125,000 points for a 5-night family trip is the Chase trifecta: Sapphire Preferred or Reserve (dining and travel), Ink Business Preferred (business spending at 3x), and Ink Business Unlimited or Cash (flat-rate earning). A family running normal spending through these cards can realistically accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually.

This sounds obvious, but adults-only Zilara properties appear in the same search results as family-friendly Ziva properties. Always confirm the property type before transferring points. Once points are transferred into Hyatt, they don't transfer back to Chase.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with a small earning or redemption every two years. A single qualifying activity — even earning 1 point through a partner — resets the clock.

Avoid Booking Refundable Rates on Points Speculatively

Some members book award stays far out with the intent to cancel, just to "hold" dates. While Hyatt does allow cancellations, this practice can strain award availability for other members and creates unnecessary complexity. Book when you're confident.

This redemption was designed — structurally, if not intentionally — for families pursuing financial independence. Here's why it fits the ChooseFI worldview so perfectly.

The ideal user is a family of three to six people who want a high-quality, genuinely relaxing vacation without the mental overhead of per-meal, per-drink, per-activity budgeting. The all-inclusive format eliminates the "should we splurge on dinner?" anxiety that can undercut vacation enjoyment. You've already "paid" with points. Just enjoy.

You need a minimum of 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night. For a realistic 5-night family trip, plan for 125,000 points — or 100,000 if you hold the World of Hyatt card and qualify for the 5th night free benefit. This is very achievable if you've been accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards through normal household spending on a Sapphire card.

This redemption is also excellent for couples celebrating anniversaries or honeymoons (use Zilara for the adults-only experience), parents of young children who want a vacation where the kids are engaged so the adults can actually relax, and travelers who want a warm-weather, beach vacation without the complexity of international award flight bookings.

This is NOT the right fit if you prefer boutique, off-the-beaten-path travel over resort-style vacations, you're a solo traveler (the per-person value scales poorly), or you're chasing ultra-premium redemptions like business class flights or city luxury hotels. The Hyatt portfolio has those too — but this specific sweet spot is about maximum family value, not maximum luxury status.

This redemption earns an **Easy** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. The ChooseFI community members who struggle with it usually hit one of two friction points, and both are easily solved. **The Earning Side: Very Easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers 1:1 to World of Hyatt instantly. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you already have access to the best transfer path. Earning 125,000 Chase UR points for a 5-night trip is a reasonable 12–18 month project for a household running normal expenses through rewards cards. **The Booking Side: Easy, With One Catch.** The Hyatt website is clean and the points booking process is straightforward. The one challenge is **peak date availability** — spring break and holiday weeks book up fast at the most popular Ziva properties. The fix is simple: use the 395-day booking window. Set a phone reminder 13 months before your target trip and search the day availability opens. **The Transfer Confidence Hurdle.** Some beginners are nervous about transferring points to Hyatt before they have a confirmed booking. The practical risk is real — if you transfer and then can't find availability, those points are stranded in Hyatt (though they're still useful for future bookings). The solution: always **confirm availability before transferring**. Hyatt lets you select dates and see the points cost before you're asked to pay. Get to that confirmation screen first, then transfer. If you can navigate a hotel booking website and move money between financial accounts, you can execute this redemption. Start with a low-stakes search on hyatt.com today — just to get comfortable with how award availability looks.

Log into your World of Hyatt account and search for all-inclusive properties at your desired destination. Filter by the Hyatt Ziva (family-friendly) or Hyatt Zilara (adults-only) brands. Check the nightly points rate — it will show the standard award rate and whether peak or off-peak pricing applies.

Check the same dates at the cash rate to calculate your cents per point value. If the cash rate is $600 per night and the award rate is 25,000 points, you are getting 2.4 cents per point. For all-inclusives, values above 2 cents per point are common and 3 or more cents per point is typical during peak season.

Transfer the required points from your Chase account to World of Hyatt. Transfers are instant. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred, you can transfer directly. Freedom and Ink Cash points can be pooled to a Sapphire card first.

Complete the booking using your World of Hyatt points. Select the standard room type on points — all-inclusive benefits apply to all room categories. Add any special requests for your family (crib, connecting rooms, dietary needs) in the booking notes.

If you have World of Hyatt Globalist status (earned at 60 nights or through the Globalist challenge), you unlock suite upgrades (subject to availability), late checkout, and other premium benefits. Even without elite status, the all-inclusive base experience is exceptional — every meal, drink, and activity is covered.

A 7-night stay at a Hyatt Ziva or Zilara typically costs 175,000 to 245,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 to 35,000 per night depending on the property and season). This covers the room, all meals, unlimited drinks, activities, and entertainment for the duration of your stay.

At Hyatt Ziva (family-friendly) properties, children typically stay and eat free when sharing a room with parents. Policies vary by property and the child's age — generally children under 12 are included at no additional cost. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only (18+). Check the specific property's policy when booking.

You can, but you will get significantly less value. The Chase portal values points at 1.25 cents (CSP) or 1.5 cents (CSR) per point. Transferring to Hyatt for an all-inclusive typically delivers 2 to 4 cents per point — roughly double the portal value. For a $600-per-night all-inclusive, the portal would cost 40,000 to 48,000 Chase points per night, while a direct Hyatt transfer costs only 25,000 points.

Most Hyatt all-inclusive award stays include resort fees in the points rate, but you may owe taxes and some incidental charges. Expect to pay $30 to $80 per night in local taxes depending on the country. Some premium experiences (spa treatments, excursions, premium alcohol) may carry additional charges. Tips for staff are at your discretion and appreciated.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Hyatt all-inclusive resorts represent the single best hotel redemption for families in the travel rewards ecosystem. The combination of a premium resort experience, all meals and drinks included, and 2 to 4 cents per point value makes this a sweet spot that is hard to beat. A family of four can enjoy a week-long beach vacation at a Hyatt Ziva for 175,000 transferable Chase points — a stay that would cost $4,000 to $7,000 in cash. For the ChooseFI community, this is the redemption that makes points tangible: your kids are splashing in the pool, you are enjoying a beachfront dinner, and the entire experience was covered by your Chase credit card rewards. Transfer to Hyatt, book early for peak dates, and give your family the vacation you have been optimizing for.

#8666. Bodybuilder AJ Ellison Shares 3 tips for Fat Loss After 50

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

IFBB Pro and Masters Men’s Physique Competitor Adam J. Ellison may be 50 years old, but he has a physique that would make most men half his age green with envy. Fortunately, the proud father of three kids says that it is still possible to drop fat while juggling the responsibilities of work and family, as he shared his “No B.S. guide” on Instagram.

AJ Ellison knows that fat mass tends to increase while lean muscle decreases with age, and science suggests that the slow down in metabolic rates could play a significant role as to why it is harder to drop body fat as we age, but that doesn’t mean that we should ditch our physique goals  as we mature. Ellison, now 50 years old, is still winning competitions on stage, and looked phenomenal as he topped the Master’s 50+ Men’s Physique category at the 2026 IFBB Masters World Championships. He even placed second in the 40+, meaning that AJ is still hanging with those who are up to a decade younger than himself. With all that in mind, here are his tips for dropping stubborn fat.

“Fat loss doesn’t start in the gym, it starts in your kitchen,” wrote Ellison. “You can’t out-train a poor diet.” The big man also said that he makes sure to consume plenty of protein. “Aim for 50 to 70g of protein at every meal. Build every plate around protein first. Fill the rest with whole foods.”

“Most men try to burn more calories. That’s backwards,” said Ellison. “Protect your muscle first.” While muscle does not burn calories directly, the presence of more muscle tissue means that there is a greater level of energy required in the body, leading to a greater calorie requirement.

To build muscle, the competitive bodybuilder suggested that we “Lift 3 to 4 times every week,” and added that for hypertrophy, “Progress your lifts whenever possible.”

“Cardio is a tool. It isn’t the foundation,” believes Ellison, who utilizes cardiovascular training to support his efforts without making it the center of his ethos. “Strength training should always come first,” wrote the master, for his almost 900K Instagram followers.

To make sure that cardio is part of the mix, “Add 8,000 to 10,000 daily steps,” enthused Ellison. “Use cardio to support recovery, not to punish yourself.”

Summing up, the bodybuilder noted that “Small calorie deficits beat aggressive diets,” observing that “Crash dieting teaches your body to conserve energy.” So, to get started, Ellison coached that we should aim to lose 0.5 to 1% of body fat per week, and to trust in the process. “Track your progress for at least three weeks before changing anything,” he concluded.

#8664. The Strongest Pre-Workout Powders to Fuel Your Training in 2025

We tested more than 80 pre-workouts and chose the strongest ones to enhance your physical and mental performance.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Whether you’re starting your fitness journey or you’re a weightlifting junkie, there are several supplements that should be staples in your stack. As a certified personal trainer and nutrition coach, I’d put a high-quality whey protein powder and one of the best creatines at the top.

Not far behind would be another supplement that can help you achieve your muscle-building and weight-loss goals: pre-workout.

However, just like not all barbells are created equal, neither are supps. The strongest pre-workouts stand out from the pack because they are formulated with research-backed doses of four key ingredients — caffeine (at least 200 milligrams), L-citrulline (at least 4,000 milligrams), beta-alanine (at least 3,200 milligrams), and betaine (at least 2,500 milligrams) — for physical and mental performance enhancement.

To save you the trouble of sipping on something that won’t give you an effective muscle pump, our team of expert product testers tried more than 80 pre-workouts and reported which supplements delivered the most focus, power, and tingles. Then, with some guidance from a few other experts, our squad of CPTs, CNCs, CrossFit enthusiasts, and dedicated weightlifters narrowed down the list to the eight strongest pre-workouts so you can select the perfect match for your goals and preferences.

Medical disclaimer: This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If your goal is to improve your athletic performance and power output in the gym, then we recommend Transparent Labs BULK BLACK. This supplement contains a potent combination of 4,000 milligrams of beta-alanine, 2,500 milligrams of betaine anhydrous, and 10 other active ingredients. Beta-alanine, a nonessential amino acid, may improve potential power output by reducing muscle fatigue, allowing you to push out a few more reps while you exercise. And studies show betaine anhydrous may improve muscular endurance. These ingredients work together to enhance your training, paving the way for strength gains over time.

Each serving of BULK BLACK also contains 350 milligrams of caffeine, which is close to the recommended daily limit of 400 milligrams. Overall, the impressive formulation earns 4 out of 5 stars from our team, as we docked a point for the high caffeine content since it may be too intense for some people.

However, this high-stim pre-workout is certainly effective.

Cory Kessler, C.P.T., C.F.N.C., has tried more than 25 pre-workouts. He tested the Blue Raspberry flavor of BULK BLACK before a cardio workout, noting that he felt more energized and focused throughout his workout. “I started sweating almost immediately, and within five to 10 minutes, I had a boost of energy, a massive pump, and felt like I could lift harder and stronger,” he says. Cory also experienced the tingling sensation common with high doses of beta-alanine.

Cory also enjoys using BULK BLACK before bodybuilding workouts since it contains 8,000 milligrams of citrulline malate. While more research is needed, some studies suggest citrulline malate may boost exercise and muscular performance.

Two other areas where BULK BLACK stands out: solubility and taste. Our team gave Transparent Labs perfect scores in both categories.

“BULK BLACK completely dissolved in my shaker bottle in only a few seconds with no clumps, grittiness, or residue,” Cory says.

Available in eight flavors ranging from Black Cherry to Watermelon Peach to Strawberry Mango, one of our other product testers chose the Blue Raspberry option, giving it 5 out of 5 stars for taste. However, there are some mixed reviews on Amazon about the taste, depending on which flavor you choose.

“It’s hard to describe the taste of Blue Raspberry, but that’s exactly what it tastes like. Not too sweet, which is a good thing,” he says.

Related: Transparent Labs BCAA Glutamine Review

Legion Pulse is our pick for the strongest natural pre-workout because it’s free from artificial sweeteners, flavors, and colors and contains six active ingredients that support enhanced energy.

As a CPT and CNC, I look for four main ingredients in a high-quality pre-workout supplement: caffeine, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, and L-citrulline. Each plays a key role in enhancing athletic performance. Research shows:

Legion Pulse contains all four, including 350 milligrams of caffeine per serving, which is very close to the recommended daily limit of 400 milligrams. Keep in mind that if you decide to try Pulse, it’s a good idea to monitor your caffeine intake from other sources like coffee or tea.

“To get the most out of pre-workout supplements without stomach issues, start with a lower dose to see how your body reacts,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, Ph.D., RD. “Choose supplements with fewer stimulants if caffeine bothers you, or go for stimulant-free options.”

Luckily, if you’re new to pre-workout or are caffeine-sensitive, you can also choose the non-stim version of Pulse. So, even though we’d like to see creatine in the formulation, we still give this a strong score of 4 out of 5 stars, especially since there’s a caffeine-free version.

One of our product testers has tried five different brands of pre-workout and puts Pulse atop her list because of its effectiveness.

“I’ve been using Pulse three times a week for six months, and it always makes me feel energized and focused,” our tester says. “My goal is to improve my personal records and lift harder, so Pulse is my go-to when I train.”

She reports that it typically takes 15 minutes for this high-stim pre-workout to kick in, and while it does give her tingles, it’s not overwhelming. “I never feel a drop-off, but rather a slow energy release,” she says.

Pulse comes in 22 flavors, including Pink Lemonade, Cherry Limeade, and Strawberry Kiwi, so there’s something to satisfy everyone’s taste buds. That said, one of our testers gave Pulse 4 out of 5 stars for taste, noting that while it tastes sweet, there’s a “weird aftertaste.”

While the formulation and flavor options make this a top-rated pre-workout, Pulse is by no means a budget-friendly option. At around $45 for a 20-serving tub, it earns the lowest score of 1 out of 5 stars for price per serving.

While many strong pre-workouts cost around $2 per serving, Nutricost Pre-X is our pick for the strongest budget pre-workout because it costs less than half of that. At about $0.93 per serving, one tester called it “the best value on the market,” and I agree, giving this a perfect score of 5 out of 5 for price per serving.

Although some budget pre-workouts lack key ingredients, Pre-X contains the four main ones we like to see in a pre-workout: caffeine, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, and L-citrulline. “The price is better than most other pre-workouts I’ve tried, especially for a supplement this good,” says one tester.

Each serving of Pre-X has 300 milligrams of caffeine and 4,000 milligrams of L-citrulline, so you should feel energized and get a good pump with this pre-workout. “I got a decent pump and had a calm focus without feeling overstimulated,” one tester says.

Some testers say Pre-X has a slightly lower dosage of beta-alanine than some other pre-workouts on our list, but others say they experienced noticeable tingles during their workout.

While testers did not experience any negative side effects when trying Pre-X, this pre-workout is made with the artificial sweetener sucralose. Some health experts have raised concerns about taking sucralose in high doses. As a CPT and someone who pays close attention to everything I put in my body, I tend to steer clear of artificial sweeteners. Because of this, we docked a point off the formulation score, giving Pre-X 4 out of 5 stars.

Nutricost Pre-X comes in five flavors, including Blue Raspberry, Peach Mango, and Watermelon. Collectively, our team gave this strong pre-workout 4.5 out of 5 stars for taste.

“This tastes great ice cold or at room temperature. I look forward to drinking it before my workouts,” says one tester who tried Blue Raspberry.

Another tester who tried Peach Mango also gave Pre-X his stamp of approval.

“No artificial sweetener taste at all. It has a nice flavor that’s not overly sweet.”

Whether you like a strong pre-workout that’s sweet, sour, fruity, or tart, Jacked Factory NitroSurge has a fit for you. With 11 options, you can stick to your favorite or keep a few flavors in rotation to keep your taste buds on their proverbial toes. Between the deep lineup and satisfying flavors, NitroSurge earned a perfect score for taste.

One of our testers tried Strawberry Margarita, and let’s just say she was more than satisfied with her sipping experience.

“It’s wildly delicious. I’d drink this by the side of the pool over ice all day.”

Another tester prefers Jacked Factory NitroSurge to some other strong pre-workouts he’s tried. “I did not like the Pink Lemonade flavor of Legion Pulse, but I would definitely use the Grape NitroSurge again,” he says.

As for its effectiveness? For one of our product testers, it took about 20 minutes to feel NitroSurge kick in. At that point, he felt like he could lift harder.

“I usually work out in the morning because I feel most rested then, but even after taking this in the afternoon, I felt ‘jacked up’ and ready to go,” he says, adding that he experienced tingles and a slight drop off, but neither was overwhelming.

Another tester who regularly takes strong pre-workouts doubled the dosage. He said he got “a bit of a boost from it” but nothing like what you’ll get from other strong pre-workouts. Ultimately, this makes NitroSurge a solid choice for beginners, as you can see how you respond to a single serving before upping it to two scoops.

Besides the taste, I like that it’s budget-friendly while still including evidence-backed ingredients, like L-citrulline, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, caffeine anhydrous, L-theanine, theobromine, and AstraGin. AstraGin, also found in Transparent Labs BULK BLACK, is a plant-based compound formulated to enhance nutrient absorption. While AstraGin is safe at 0.5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day, more research is needed on the potential performance-enhancing benefits.

Like some of the other pre-workouts on our list, NitroSurge is made with the artificial sweetener sucralose, which some health experts have raised concerns about taking in high doses. Also, Jacked Factory supplements do not undergo third-party testing, which ensures products include the ingredients listed on the label and nothing else. This is especially important for athletes who undergo drug testing for banned substances. We only gave Nitrosurge 3 out of 5 stars in this category since it is made in a Current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP)-certified and FDA-registered facility.

For bodybuilders, a “pump” is a sign of a successful training session. Increased blood flow to the muscles makes them feel fuller and appear larger and more vascular during and after a workout. A pump also promotes muscle growth by delivering essential nutrients and oxygen to the muscles as blood flow increases. While you can achieve a pump through high-rep sets, drop sets, and supersets, high-stim pre-workouts like Gorilla Mode are specially designed to improve your pump.

Gorilla Mode contains several pump-enhancing ingredients in each scoop, including 5,000 milligrams of pure L-citrulline (more per scoop than any other pre-workout on our list) and 2,000 milligrams of Hydro Prime glycerol powder. L-citrulline works to widen blood vessels, increasing blood flow to the muscles. Glycerol powder is rapidly absorbed by the muscles and draws in water, which can cause muscle cell swelling.

If you’re caffeine-sensitive or budget-conscious, this intense pre-workout may not be the best for you. Although one serving only contains 200 milligrams of caffeine, you will need to take two servings to get research-backed doses of some key ingredients, including creatine monohydrate (only 2.5 gram per serving). At that point, you’d be at 400 milligrams of caffeine, which is the total amount the FDA says is safe for adults to consume per day. For this reason, we docked a point off the formulation, giving Gorilla Mode 4 out of 5 stars in this category.

Don’t forget that this also impacts how much bang you get for your buck. A 40-serving tub costs $60, and you’ll end up going through it that much quicker if you take two scoops before your training sessions. That would bring the cost to $3 per serving. So, from a value standpoint, we can only give Gorilla Mode 2.5 out of 5 stars.

On the other hand, this pricey supplement earned a strong score of 4.5 out of 5 stars for its effectiveness. One of our testers uses strong pre-workouts several times a week and tried Gorilla Mode before an upper-body workout. “Not only did I have a good pump, I also felt more focused. I knocked out a few more reps than usual during my workout,” he says. “I like the Fruit Punch flavor, although it was sweeter than I thought it would be.”

While our tester enjoyed Gorilla Mode’s taste, he says the powder was gritty and difficult to mix properly. This is likely due to the glycerol powder, which absorbs moisture, leading to clumping.

If you like feeling skin tingles after taking your pre-workout, check out Crazy Nutrition Intensive Pre-Train. I love the prickly skin sensation because it lets me know my pre-workout is kicking in and it’s time to train. This temporary side effect, called paresthesia, is caused by beta-alanine, which works to increase muscular endurance.

Intensive Pre-Train has 3,500 milligrams of beta-alanine per serving, which is more per serving than almost all of the other pre-workouts on our list. “Beta-alanine is found in most pre-workout supplements, likely because it helps reduce fatigue and improve endurance in the short term,” says registered dietitian Alex Oskian. “This is because it reduces acidity in the body, which comes from lactic acid build-up.”

Our product tester used Crazy Nutrition Intensive Pre-Train before a high-intensity interval training (HIIT) workout and felt the tingles within 15 minutes. “These were strong compared to some other pre-workouts I’ve tried,” he says. “I felt good tingles in my hands and face, which lasted for about an hour.”

Earning a 5 out of 5 for effectiveness, Intense Pre-Train is also available in a caffeine-free version for those who don’t want stimulants in their pre-workout. The non-stim version comes in Green Apple, which our tester says tasted more like a greens powder than a sour apple.

“I’m rather caffeine-dependent, so I didn’t feel a burst of energy. I prefer caffeinated pre-workouts, but this is a great option for a late-night lifting session,” she says. Other testers who tried the Fruit Punch flavor say they enjoyed the tangy taste. To enhance the flavor, Crazy Nutrition is sweetened with the artificial sweetener sucralose. With some mixed reviews on the different flavors, we give this pre-workout a 3.5 out of 5 for taste.

Onnit Alpha Brain is designed to increase mental acuity and focus. Testers say that’s exactly how they felt after trying Onnit Alpha Brain, which is why it’s our pick for the strongest pre-workout for focus.“What makes this pre-workout stand out is the cognitive effects. I felt significantly more focused after taking Alpha Brain than any other pre-workout I’ve tried,” says one of our testers.

Other testers agreed, saying Alpha Brain helped them feel present and ready to work out without being overstimulated, leading to an effectiveness score of 4 out of 5 stars.

Onnit Alpha Brain’s formula differs from most other strong pre-workout supplements on our list — it contains nootropics, substances that enhance learning and memory. One of the key ingredients, NooGandha, is an ashwagandha extract that can reduce stress and enhance well-being by reducing cortisol levels in the body.

Another key ingredient, AlphaSize, may promote the production of acetylcholine, a powerful neurotransmitter that enhances cognitive function. However, studies demonstrating the effect of alpha-GPC on cognitive performance used 200 to 400 milligram doses per day, and a serving of Onnit Alpha brain has 125 milligrams.

The other unique ingredient in Onnit Alpha Brain is Dynamine. It works similarly to caffeine, by blocking the body’s adenosine receptors that cause you to feel tired. However, this ingredient is banned in all sports supplements in Australia. While Dynamine is still allowed for sports competitions in the U.S., it is possible it will be banned in the future. Competitive athletes may want to steer clear of this product.

One of our testers says Alpha Brain is only middle-of-the-road compared to other strong pre-workouts when it comes to physical energy. “After taking other strong pre-workouts, I usually experience a boost in energy. After taking this pre-workout, the mental effects were much more noticeable than the physical ones,” she says. That may be in part because Alpha Brain lacks ingredients like betaine anhydrous, taurine, and creatine, which can support muscle growth and recovery.

We give the formulation 4 out of 5 stars thanks to the inclusion of nootropics, which are quickly becoming more prevalent in the supplement market. But be aware that this probably isn’t your best bet for boosting your physical energy levels.

Long before the days of gummy and ready-to-drink (RTD) pre-workout options, the most popular choice was the original C4. The latest version, C4 Ultimate, is more concentrated than the classic formula, combining both exercise performance and cognitive-enhancing ingredients.

One of our testers tried C4 Ultimate before a 30-minute HIIT workout, reporting that the caffeine blend got her zoned in before her training.

“I felt great throughout the entire workout,” she reported, giving C4 Ultimate a perfect score for effectiveness.

This high-stim pre-workout is sweetened with sucralose, which some health experts have raised concerns about. While our tester doesn’t mind a very sweet pre-workout, the Icy Blue Razz flavor was a little too sugary for her liking. Mixing it in more water than recommended balances out the sweetness.

However, another tester was blown away by the Sour Batch Bros flavor, saying it tasted “just like Sour Patch Kids.” Taking both of their experiences into consideration, we’ll meet in the middle and give C4 Ultimate a 4 out of 5 for taste, especially since it comes in multiple flavors.

Another plus for this product: It contains creatine — a popular supplement among athletes and bodybuilders for its ability to boost strength, enhance recovery, and prevent injury. Because of its performance-enhancing capabilities, some people like to take creatine in addition to their pre-workout. If you want the best of both worlds, we recommend C4 Ultimate.

Keep in mind that one serving contains 1.5 grams of creatine per serving, which is less than the recommended value of 3 to 5 grams daily. If you want to get the most performance-enhancing benefits from creatine, you should invest in a standalone supplement to help support your fitness goals.One final note: If you compete in a sport that requires drug testing, C4 Ultimate may not be the best strong pre-workout for you because it’s made with Dynamine, which is currently banned for use in Australia.

Our team of expert testers includes certified personal trainers, nutrition coaches, and CrossFit enthusiasts. As dedicated lifters and lovers of all things health and fitness, we’ve collectively tried more than 80 pre-workouts, giving us a broad perspective of what’s available on the market.

We tested each supplement before a workout, and in some cases, for several weeks or months, to evaluate its performance-enhancing benefits, taste, and whether the supplement had any negative side effects.

Using a 1-5 scoring system, we rated each pre-workout on a variety of factors, including:

At the end of the testing period, we compared feedback to whittle our list down to only the best of the best. We also received valuable input from nutrition experts on what makes a strong pre-workout.

A strong pre-workout contains a combination of performance-enhancing ingredients in research-backed dosages. “Usually, the strength of a pre-workout is based upon the amount of stimulants it contains. High doses of caffeine (300+ milligrams) are usually a quick identifier of the pre-workout’s strength,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian says.

However, the potency of a pre-workout goes beyond the caffeine content. Other active ingredients like L-citrulline, beta-alanine, and betaine anhydrous can impact energy, focus muscular endurance, and power output.

“Stronger via the amount of caffeine isn’t always better. If the goal is a bigger pump in the gym, other ingredients like L-citrulline may be better,” says Alex. “Another common ingredient that can help a pre-workout feel stronger is beta-alanine, which may cause a tingling or ‘pins and needles’ sensation on the skin.”

It’s also important to remember that “strong” is a subjective term. For example, I can handle a full scoop of RedCon1 Total War without a problem, but I have friends who get too many tingles from a single serving.

“Everyone’s body reacts differently to various compounds, so what works for one person might not be best for another,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, Ph.D., RD.

A strong, well-dosed pre-workout supplement may help you train harder by boosting your energy, focus, and endurance during intense workouts.

“There are a few things that are really helpful when you are looking for a great gym session: energy to do the work, mental clarity to help focus on what you are doing (not just to work the muscle, but to prevent injury), and a great workout,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian says. “Using a pre-workout may just help you achieve all of these.”

Let’s explore the potential benefits of taking a strong pre-workout before you start your training session.

Caffeine is one of the most popular stimulants used in pre-workout supplements to enhance energy levels and improve focus. Almost all of the pre-workouts on our list use caffeine and L-theanine. Studies have shown when paired with caffeine, L-theanine may improve cognitive performance.

“Most pre-workouts contain the stimulant caffeine in higher dosages. L-theanine helps counteract the unwanted effects of caffeine supplementation: jittery feelings and a post-caffeine crash,” Alex says. “You might see less mental fatigue, improved reaction time, and fewer headaches while regularly supplementing with L-theanine.”

I like taking a pre-workout to improve my focus because it helps intensify my workout and keep me #lockedin. Several pre-workouts on our list contain Alpha-GPC and tyrosine to give you that zoned-in feeling. Research suggests Alpha-GPC may improve cognitive function, and tyrosine may increase dopamine levels and cognition. One study found L-tyrosine helped improve people’s memory while they worked on a demanding task.

A pre-workout may help you squeeze out a few more reps as you work to build strength and muscle. Two ingredients commonly used in pre-workout, beta-alanine and betaine anhydrous, may help reduce fatigue and support muscular endurance.

“Research suggests betaine anhydrous can improve muscle strength and power via increased total work capacity and improved protein synthesis within the body. Simply put, you can do more work, which leads to increased strength and muscle growth,” says Alex.

Another common ingredient, taurine, may improve your performance and power.

Registered dietitian Alex Oskian says not every pre-workout is created equal, so it’s important to pay attention to what’s on the label. “Supplements are not regulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This means the supplement might not contain all the ingredients you’re looking for and may even contain unwanted ingredients,” she says. Alex recommends looking for supplements that undergo third-party testing.

If you choose a high-stim pre-workout, be mindful of your caffeine intake from other sources like coffee, tea, or soda so that you don’t go over the daily recommended value of 400 milligrams. This will help prevent potential negative side effects like jitters, anxiety, or trouble falling asleep.

“Consuming caffeine at the end of your day may cause sleep disturbances, which only hurts performance in the long run,” says Oskian.

No matter which pre-workout you choose, it’s important to follow the recommended intake guidelines. Remember, pre-workouts should not be taken more than once per day.

“Pre-workout supplements are generally safe for healthy adults, but they can have some potential side effects,” says Dr. Raj Dasgupta, MD, FACP, FCCP, FAASM. “It is important to start with a low dose and talk to your doctor before taking them, especially if you have any underlying health conditions.”

There are a number of important factors to consider when deciding which strong pre-workout is right for you, including:

Many strong pre-workouts incorporate a variety of active ingredients. When choosing a pre-workout supplement, consider your goals. For example, a bodybuilder may prefer a pre-workout powder that’s highly caffeinated and contains ingredients such as L-citrulline, betaine anhydrous, and creatine to help improve performance. On the other hand, an endurance athlete may want a pre-workout that has less caffeine but includes beta-alanine, BCAAs, and mineral electrolytes.

Whenever possible, I choose supplements that are tested by a third party for purity and have transparent labeling. Athletes who undergo drug testing should look for certifications from Informed Choice and NSF, which ensure the product does not include any banned substances.

Although we test all of the products we recommend, it’s important to check out customer reviews, especially from people with similar fitness goals and preferences. They can provide valuable insights into the product’s overall effectiveness, potential side effects, and the most popular flavors.

“Recommended brands and products are ones that are highly rated by users and contain ingredients that have been backed by scientific research,” says Dr. Raj Dasgupta.

“Taste plays a big role in pre-workout selection. If you don’t like a particular flavor, then you likely won’t drink the pre-workout no matter its benefits,” Oskian says. It’s also important to consider the use of artificial flavors, colors, and sweeteners.

The price of a pre-workout doesn’t necessarily reflect its effectiveness. Understanding the ingredients list and dosage levels is important to ensure you’re paying for a high-quality supplement and not just expensive marketing.

There are a few potential red flags you want to avoid when picking out a pre-workout.

I like to avoid supplements made using proprietary blends. These blends are combinations of ingredients, but the individual doses are not fully disclosed. This lack of transparency makes it impossible to assess the effectiveness and safety of the supplement.

Many fitness enthusiasts and athletes prefer all-natural ingredients and products free from unnecessary fillers or additives. “If sugar alcohols and artificial sweeteners wreak havoc on your stomach, make sure those aren’t on the ingredient list,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian says.

Athletes who compete in sanctioned organizations should make sure the supplements they use are third-party tested and certified banned substance-free.

If you have big fitness goals, choosing a strong pre-workout formulated with safe and effective doses of science-backed ingredients is worth it to deliver performance-enhancing effects. Keep in mind that even the strongest pre-workouts on the market won’t make you run faster, lift heavier, or exercise longer on their own. These supplements are designed to help you put in the work at the gym to make gains and enhance your performance over time.

Ultimately, though, a strong pre-workout is only part of the equation to becoming the strongest version of yourself. At the end of the day, you have to put in the work, follow a sound nutrition plan, and prioritize rest and recovery to crush your fat-burning and muscle-building goals.

Yes, technically, you can take a pre-workout made with 400 milligrams of caffeine. However, that is the maximum daily dose recommended by the FDA. This means if you’re using a high-stim pre-workout, you may want to avoid caffeine from other sources like coffee, tea, soda, or energy drinks. Since 400 milligrams is the maximum recommended daily dose, I do not advise using a pre-workout containing 600 milligrams of caffeine.

A pre-workout can directly and indirectly make you stronger. A well-dosed pre-workout may help you add a few pounds to your lifts or allow you to push out a few more reps during your workout. However, real strength gains will come from consistent training, proper nutrition, and recovery. If a pre-workout supplement helps you stay consistent in the gym, it may also help you gain strength and muscle mass.

Yes. Depending on your sensitivity to stimulants like caffeine, you may experience side effects, including jitters, anxiety, or difficulty falling asleep. If this is the case, use a half serving or a more moderately dosed pre-workout to assess your tolerance.

Stephen is an ISSA-certified personal trainer and nutritionist with an immense passion for health and fitness. A two-time University of Florida graduate and longtime rugby player, he brings more than a decade of strength training experience, plus a diverse writing and editing background. When he’s not creating content or hitting the gym, he enjoys traveling, cooking, and attending music festivals around the world.
