Planning ahead is the key, applying principles mentioned in this blog and our paper. We all have worked so hard…..we deserve a great retirement.

great article…great advice. As the offspring of depression era parents, I was taught (by example) early to be thrifty and save. When burnout came at age 62, I was ready and haven’t looked back. My only regret is being too conservative with my investments, but then again being more aggressive would have forced me to hang on some extra years after the 2008 market crash.

I am so sorry, you lost me at the fact that you actually were burning 35k per month!!! how is that even possible!!! you are exactly where you chose to be, its consequences. Most of us, and I honestly believe I speak for the majority of physicians, do not even get remotely close to such an exaggerated figure. Most of us have limited our spending as our reimbursement has declined. Many of us have actually struggled even keeping a low profile and living with economic restraints. I stopped reading at that figure because it is just absurd.

I appreciate you taking the time to comment, even if you stopped reading at the $35K figure. Let me address your skepticism directly, because you’re right to be shocked—and that’s exactly the point. When I wrote this article, I had a word count limit on how much I could disclose on the background of Doctor Addams (who is really a he). What I did not go into detail about is how he arrived at where he is today. It’s not one absurd decision. It’s twenty years of reasonable-sounding decisions that compound like interest you can’t afford.

Dr. Addams didn’t wake up one day and decide to burn through $420K annually. He made decisions that seemed perfectly justified at each step. I would not have discovered what my friend was going through had I not asked him to invest in my startup back then. He then confided how illiquid he was and how much in a hole he was in.

The reality is that our monthly expenses are not the usual discussion physicians talk about in the physicians’ lounge. It’s really very personal, so I get it that this sounds absurd, but the reality is that there is a lot of shame ascribed to our salaries when we really aren’t visibly successful. So why would we share it? Which may explain why it sounds so absurd to you. Sadly, he is not the first person in such a financial hole since its more common than you think. So what happened?

His surgical group was thriving pre-COVID. She was making $400K+ and felt secure in budgeting for this lifestyle. Then the floor dropped:

Insurance reimbursements got slashed Hospital-based specialty groups ate their market share

His income dropped to $280K, then $240K (he was already burned out from trying to get bigger dividends he had to do more call, which was not sustainable. Yeah, many private groups make these kind of dead-end deals)

What happened next? He did not scale back his lifestyle because he was optimistic about his future. I don’t have the space here to list his expenses but what I remember after a very emotional and stressful session was that his parents were aging and he had to help financially. His sister-in-law had a business that he helped with some capital, which became a recurring theme. All these decisions are made with good intentions, but they add up. He leased a really nice car and could not figure out how to back out of that deal.

The real lesson: This story isn’t about judgment. It’s about prevention. Every physician should see this and think: “Could this happen to me with just 3-4 different decisions?”

Because here’s the truth: The distance between financial security and financial disaster for a high-earning physician is about five bad decisions over twenty years. That’s it.

Your restraint is admirable. But I wrote this article for the physicians who haven’t shown that restraint yet—and who still have time to fix it before they’re staring at a retirement calculator at age 58.

The $35K isn’t absurd. It’s terrifyingly more common (than you think) among physicians who started making big money without a financial plan. If this article makes even one physician audit their spending before it’s too late, it was worth writing—and worth your discomfort reading it.

As someone who spends at 30k per month, let me help with this: $2500 per month goes to an aging parent on one side, $2000 to an aging parent on the other. 3.5k per month goes to a vacation home mortgage and expenses, although it has appreciated enough over time that that will be eventually recovered. Travel is a big one as our 6 children and 6 grandchildren live all over the place, and flights, airport parking etc are $5000 per month. Life insurance is a big one, at 2k per month, health for myself is only $600 per month but it’s $1500 for my wife. I’ll stop there, but we are not driving fancy cars and our primary residence is only worth 330k, hardly a mansion. I retired with over 6 million NW and 60k in pension/ss, which will probably cover it: once the elderly parents have passed it should work out, but we might have to sell the vacation house when we are older.

This should be required reading for every resident – and required re-reading every year of residency and beyond! I appreciate the comments about spouses being involved in all finances – that goes for us, too! Many of us are married to high-earners who manage their own (and sometimes our) finances and find out too late that they were terrible at it.

Thank you! You’re absolutely right—this should be mandatory reading starting in residency, before the income jump happens and the mistakes become expensive.

Your point about spouses needing to be involved cuts both ways, and it’s critical. I’ve sat with too many people who discovered their high-earning spouse was: – Flying blind with no actual plan – Paying 2% in fees to an advisor who was just collecting checks – Invested in their buddy’s restaurant/startup/crypto scheme – Carrying three whole life insurance policies they didn’t understand – Making $400K but somehow living paycheck to paycheck

Financial competence doesn’t correlate with income or intelligence. A physician making $500K can be just as clueless as anyone else—sometimes more so, because the high income masks the problems until it’s too late.

Being involved doesn’t mean you need to manage everything. It means you know where the accounts are, understand the plan, can access everything if needed, and serve as that crucial second set of eyes. Your spouse’s overconfidence plus your informed questions might prevent a catastrophic mistake.

Money is a team sport. Whether you’re the earner or the spouse, staying informed and involved isn’t optional—it’s survival.

The freedom you describe—loving medicine because you can retire whenever you want—that’s what happens when you get the math right early. You avoided the nightmare by doing exactly what Dr. Addams eventually learned: live below your means, ignore the Joneses, and make the boring financial moves that actually work.

#8549. Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

The value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

Is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

As one reader recently asked me in an email:

“The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”

To answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:

A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

When you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

If the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

Your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

But if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

Now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment)

But in that same time period, your share of company earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com

In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

So as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

That doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

But Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

Let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a big Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

This is exactly why the price of an individual company’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

But what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more quickly?

In the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 big companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

These are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45)

If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

There’s one common theme in the big tech company boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

But that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a new era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

They may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

Having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

But the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

While the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

So What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

As I said earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:

Our economy will continue to grow and company earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies

Everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

For starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:

Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:

Wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

Just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

Longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

So far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

It’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

Over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

If you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

Another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

Then reinvest that time that everyone else spends worrying into enjoying more time engaged in hard physical stuff in the great outdoors. That’s the only place where you’ll get guaranteed market-beating returns, every time.

Is Buy and Hold Always the Best Strategy? History Says… Not Always. Yes, over the last few decades, the buy-and-hold strategy has worked incredibly well, with U.S. stock markets delivering strong returns. But that hasn’t always been the case. There have been entire decades where buy and hold yielded little to no real returns—or worse.

The 1930s: The Great Depression saw the Dow Jones lose nearly 90% of its value from 1929 to 1932. Even though the market eventually recovered, it took 25 years (until 1954) for stocks to fully regain their pre-crash levels.

The 1970s: Stagflation (high inflation + stagnant growth) crushed stock returns. The S&P 500 gained only 5% total from 1969 to 1979, which was a negative real return after inflation.

The 2000s: After the Dot-Com bubble burst in 2000 and the Financial Crisis of 2008, the S&P 500 produced negative total returns from 2000 to 2009—dubbed the “Lost Decade” for stocks.

While stocks historically tend to rise over long periods, these examples show that timing, valuation, and diversification matter. Simply buying and holding without considering macroeconomic conditions or valuations can lead to lost decades for investors

Mr. Money Mustache February 25, 2025, 10:34 am

Some of those stories about past periods of low stock returns are true, but I encourage readers to remember three more things:

1) They are usually cherry picked, for example starting from the exact peak of the 1929 bubble. In reality, investors at the time had probably accumulated most of their investments at lower prices, so they were net-positive far sooner than 1954

2) Many of the analyses you see online happen to leave out the most important reason we own stocks in the long run: DIVIDENDS – so ensure that any past simulations you run are using a data set that includes dividends (Nick Maggiulli from Of Dollars and Data is a great author who understands this: https://ofdollarsanddata.com/sp500-calculator/)

3) It’s easy to tell stories about the past and imagine that we all have a crystal ball. But remember that people back then had NO IDEA when the crash would come. In fact, I have been receiving emails non-stop since I 2013, shortly after I started writing this blog stating that it’s “time to go to cash because the market is overvalued”. In retrospect, not only our share prices but our economic growth and company earnings have been spectacular since then.

And perhaps most importantly 4) Ten years is a TINY time horizon to be thinking about investment performance for FIRE people. I’m personally less than a third of the way through my seventy year retirement, so I think in much longer time periods. A 10-15 year stretch of minimal stock growth is all built into the safety margin.

There is definitely a limit to how much a nation can safely borrow as a percentage of GDP. But this is very different from the crap the politicians sling around to rile up their base and justify cutting the programs they just happen to dislike for ideological reasons.

In a worldwide currency and debt market like we have, if you borrow too much the market sends you a signal in the form of lower demand for your dollars which leads to a decline in your currency’s value. Then you need to offer higher interest rates in order to keep borrowing money.

In recent decades the US has had the opposite “problem” – we issue higher and higher amounts of debt for sale, and buyers keep vacuuming it up which keeps our dollar strong. So like a drunk teen at the liquor store with his Mom’s credit card, we keep taking advantage of the free sauce.

To the extent that our government uses this borrowed money to build infrastructure that actually helps our country: transportation networks, ports, power production, educating our populace, even incentivizing things like Arizona semiconductor fabs, we are actually getting ahead because we are using other people’s money to build our own wealth.

It can also help to use this implicit subsidy to just lower taxes on businesses and average workers, because this will trigger more company formation and wealth and employment.

But if we go too far and see our dollar drop more than we want *or* lose our status as the world’s reserve currency, we will have to go on a serious spending diet.

But the issue is best discussed by a group of well trained economists and business leaders with a set of spreadsheets rather than a shouting political candidate at a rally.

The best approach is somewhere in between: run a sensible budget, but also bend the rules a bit and borrow a safe amount for the long run to continue juicing our own economy.

The results were cherry picked except for the people that retired at the start of those periods. For them it was real!

For the early ’70s retiree, the 4% rule just about held up, but with little margin for error. Wade Pfau’s international study found that for a 50/50 portfolio in U.S. history, 4% was roughly the “Safemax” (worst-case sustainable rate) – it survived about 30 years by the skin of its teeth, supporting only ~29 years of inflation-adjusted withdrawals in the most challenging stretch​ RETIREMENTRESEARCHER.COM . In practical terms, this means a 4% initial withdrawal did eventually work out for a 1970s retiree but only because subsequent decades (the 1980s and 1990s) were very strong. The retiree would have seen their nest egg shrink alarmingly in the first 5–10 years, likely coming close to depletion by the early 1980s, before the tide turned. T. Rowe Price analysts, for instance, note that a 1973 retiree’s portfolio (with a roughly 4% starting withdrawal) began at $500k, sank to ~$328k by 1974, but then recovered to over $500k by 1982 and ultimately grew to over $1 million by the end of 30 years​ TROWEPRICE.COM ​ TROWEPRICE.COM . In hindsight the 4% rule “worked” for that retiree – but if inflation had stayed high longer or if the 1980s boom had been weaker, the outcome could have been a failure.

It’s not a coincidence that the 4% rule just barely worked for 1970s retirees. That was the worst time period for investors in the 20th century, and 4% was chosen because it’s the maximum withdrawal rate that survived even that period.

The thing that I find interesting is all the doomsayers (i.e., those prognosticating some sort of nigh-apocalyptic destruction of the stock market) seem to operate under this bizarre assumption that the behemoths (i.e., the Magnificent 7 and others near the top of the pile) are just going to sit there and allow themselves to get trampled by some upstart. Or that they will just shrug their shoulders, say something like “well, I guess it was fun while it lasted, time to pack up the toys and go home” and then it will all be over.

Will there be disruption? Absolutely! Will it somehow upend the US stock market? I highly doubt that. The companies in the S&P 500 are economic engines, and their fuel is not just natural resources from Canada, Brazil, and Russia, but also other smaller companies. As soon as some small company comes along with a potentially disruptive change, you will absolutely see the big boys try to get in on the game (both by attempting to acquire the upstart, and also by starting or accelerating their own efforts in that space).

There is a good chance that some of the economic benefit will be “lost” (i.e., those who get in early will reap an outsized gain, while those of us index-only investors will have to wait for that disruptive technology to go mainstream), but in the end that disruptive technology will become *part* of the engine of our economy, rather than wrecking it.

My question is what happens in countries where monopolies control those things and stomp out competition due to undue bought influence from the government? In that case, the naturally self-correcting mechanisms don’t work, and political capital controls the top companies, rather than true innovation driving the market.

I suppose those companies would still be making record profits, though, so it may be a moot point.

I think there is an issue with the data of that study Howard Mark’s quotes?

It’s the J.P. Morgan Asset Management, has a square for each month from 1988 through late 2014, and then shows the subsequent 10 year returns based on entry PE. The problem is that there aren’t that many 10-year periods in that time to make that claim, and that all of them are rolling it month to month, so the 324 observations are not really 324, but actually the same 10-year period multiple times since they’re not independent.

But I agree that the logic does make sense though that higher PEs should be lower returns intuitively.

Y axis is S&P500. On x-axis, Year 0 means “right now”. The x-axis means “future”. The red line starts below yellow and blue because stocks are overvalued, i.e. have a higher P/E. The red shows what S&P SHOULD BE if P/E was typical, not very high as it is now. Basically, if the market crashed right now and reversed to a normal P/E. The blue line shows what S&P would be in the future if the current trends continue (unlikely). As mentioned above, the red line shows what S&P future will be if stocks would suddenly revert to a typical P&E now. The yellow line is similar to the red line, but shows a more gradual reversal to typical P/Es, over time. M&Ms point is that even the worse case scenario – red line – is still pretty good.

The real kicker? About 70% of the stocks are European. I barely own any US stocks.

The results: My own hand picked 20 stocks have done better than the S&P500.

I’m not a great stock picker. I didn’t invest in NVidia, Google, AMD. I sold Tesla at a loss before it went time 20. I still hold a 50% on a significant Intel stake. I stuck to Europe while the US outperformed. And yet, my returns have beaten the S&P500.

There are some great stocks in Europe. There is also a lot of not so great stocks. Picking the great ones isn’t hard. Most can see the bad ones from far away and avoid them like the plague.

The real problem for Europe, is the lack of representative indexes. The European indexes just simply suck. Not enough stocks in them. Every country has their own indexes of just a few stocks. And maybe an even bigger underappreciated problem comparing the US to the EU: dividends. The US companies barely pay dividends, while EU companies still pay a good deal. The difference adds up over the years, but most indexes don’t compare the total return.

As for these high markets: please keep in mind: we’ve had some serious inflation. Inflation adjusted returns over the last years aren’t out of the ordinary. Especially comparing inflation adjusted returns to something like a zero risk tips ladder.

Your S&P500 without the magnificent seven looks less impressive. But instead of taking out the best performers, maybe do the same but also take out the absolute worst performers. And then do both. You might be surprised to learn the whole market is actually doing really pretty well.

Conclusion: I’m really not worried. Taking a broader look and accounting for inflation and zero risk treasuries, returns aren’t extraordinary. We live in a world where in one generation, huge countries go from poor to rich, and they all want stable investments for their retirements. We live in an age where a growing number of retires will keep demand high because they don’t have to fear for their incomes. House payments look high, but the total mortgage debt in many western countries is actually quite low.

If there ever was a golden age, it’s now. We’re deadsmack in the middle of the best economic boom in history, and it doesn’t seem to be ending anytime soon (if you take a worldwide broad look). Don’t focus too much on the numbers. Look around the world, see how much things are improving in just one generation world wide. You can only conclude demand for stocks will keep increasing, and companies will keep improving profits as demand keeps increasing. Will there be shock and crashes? Sure, but nothing to worry about for a early retiree.

I also like to think of the property pay down as an after tax return, since you need to earn the money first , then pay taxes to pay the mortgage.

On the US vs International shares, people recommending to stay US only, I wonder if there’s bias because the US has done well and whether that position would’ve been very different if we were looking at a period where US had seen a weak decade, like post 08?

Having started investing in real estate before the 18% mtg rates, then watch my collegues sweat out Black Monday Oct 19/87, Iam glad we stayed 100% RE. Passive income allowed me to retire in 1998 & over the years we have also unloaded many high cap. appreciated investment properties, often holding the notes @ 10-12% with a 5yr balloon. We still buy using cash from our 401(k)-solos. Real Esatate has been our ‘annuity’ & has outperformed most of those we know who have invested heavily in the equities market. Over the years the odd bad tenant, bloodied knuckles & rehab costs have never been as stressful as our friends who said they refused to look at their 401(k)’s as the mkt swooned. All have since worked until their late 60’s. In fact my business consultant, equities investor friend, who told us we would go broke in real estate, suffers very poor health & still has to work at 70. Thanks to my wife all of our kids are heavily invested in real estate & have enough passive income to cover their respective mortgages.

One last thing I like to check in on for any wealthier investors reading this: make sure you continue to question your old habits as your wealth grows.

My first patient was already dead. She arrived zipped in a vinyl bag, smelling of formaldehyde and phenol, and she taught me more anatomy in one semester than any lecturer managed in four years.

Somewhere between the first incision and the nervous jokes about her coral nail polish, I figured out that the human body runs stranger than the textbook admits. The mind bolted to it runs stranger still.

The years since have only confirmed the suspicion. Some of what I’ve seen belongs in a haunted house. The rest belongs in a haunted house with a billing department.

For Halloween this year, I’m recalling some of the odd things about being human you learn as a physician over the years.

Retirement is optional for the dead. Donated bodies pick up second careers the day their first one ends. At Wayne State University in Detroit, cadavers have ridden impact sleds for decades so engineers could learn what a steering column does to a sternum when a sedan meets a bridge abutment.

Seatbelts, airbags, and padded dashboards all carry the fingerprints of people who signed a donor form and then absorbed the kind of blow no living volunteer would accept. Count the people who walk away from highway crashes today, and a fair share owe a thank-you note to somebody in a body bag.

My cadaver spent her retirement teaching a roomful of first-years how a hand works. Meanwhile I spend Tuesday afternoons on hold with a prior authorization line. She was more productive, and she never billed.

Nothing in residency prepared me for the cadaver head course. Severed heads rested face up in disposable roasting pans, lined down a row of tables, while surgeons calmly rehearsed facelifts. I kept my coffee down, though it was close.

Consider the advantages. These patients won’t ask about downtime or bring up a cousin’s botched eyelid job, and the state board will hear nothing from them. Somebody should study their satisfaction scores.

Medicine has always practiced on the dead, and for a long stretch it practiced on dead people who never agreed to the arrangement.

Nineteenth-century anatomy schools bought corpses from grave robbers and asked few questions about provenance. In Edinburgh in 1828, William Burke and William Hare decided digging was too slow, murdered sixteen people, and sold the bodies to anatomist Robert Knox.

Britain answered with the Anatomy Act of 1832, which handed medical schools the unclaimed bodies of the poor. Reform, of a sort.

Physicians have spent centuries trying to pin down the second a person stops being a person. We have never once nailed it.

In 1905, a French doctor named Beaurieux stood beside the guillotine as a convict named Languille lost his head. Beaurieux called out the man’s name. By his own report, the eyelids lifted and the eyes fixed on him before closing, and the trick worked a second time before it quit for good.

Consciousness or reflex? Nobody could say then, and we can’t now.

Cleveland, 1970. Neurosurgeon Robert White transplanted the head of one rhesus monkey onto the body of another, and the head woke up and tracked people around the room. White spent the rest of his career insisting the operation could work in humans.

I met my own version of this riddle at the bedside of a brain-dead organ donor. He was warm and pink. His heart pumped, his kidneys made urine, and at one point a spinal reflex lifted his arm off the sheet, the move clinicians call the Lazarus sign.

The nurse beside me didn’t flinch. I did. Legally he had died hours earlier, and the procurement team was already en route.

Hospice taught me the rest. Dying unfolds over hours or days, a slow dimming no monitor captures cleanly, yet the death certificate demands a single timestamp. So we pick one and move on.

For several centuries, European apothecaries sold ground-up mummy as medicine. Physicians prescribed it for bruises, bleeding and a long menu of complaints, and when genuine Egyptian stock ran short, enterprising suppliers manufactured fresh “mummy” from whatever bodies they could find.

Folklore adds “mellified man,” a corpse supposedly steeped in honey for a century and sold by the chunk. Historians doubt he ever existed. I’ve seen supplement labels make bolder claims.

The dead, for all their weirdness, behave predictably. They stay where you put them. The living refuse that courtesy.

Beginning in the early 2000s, hundreds of children in Sweden withdrew into a state that looked like coma. Nearly all came from asylum-seeking families facing deportation.

They quit eating and talking, then quit opening their eyes, and some stayed that way for a year or longer while parents turned them in bed and nurses ran their feeding tubes. Swedish doctors named it uppgivenhetssyndrom. Resignation syndrome.

Scans came back clean, and so did the labs. Nobody found a virus, a toxin or a lesion. The condition clustered almost entirely inside Swedish borders, and many of the children surfaced slowly once their families won permission to stay.

That makes a lot of physicians squirm. The suffering is real, the paralysis is real, and the driver is a mind expressing despair in the shape its surroundings taught it to take.

I’ve watched a milder version play out in hospice more times than I can count. A patient holds steady for weeks, the family meeting goes sideways, and by the next morning he has stopped eating.

In the Kazakh village of Kalachi, starting around 2013, residents began dozing off mid-sentence. Some slept for days and woke with no memory of it. A shuttered Soviet uranium mine sat down the road, which made for a tidy villain.

Officials tested the air, water and soil, and the government eventually relocated much of the town. Plenty of clinicians point instead to a community watching its jobs and young people drain away, taking any sense of a future with them.

Le Roy, New York, ran a similar script in 2011. A cluster of high school girls developed tics, jerks and verbal outbursts that spread through the school and lit up the evening news.

Erin Brockovich showed up to investigate a chemical spill from a 1970 train derailment. Neurologists diagnosed conversion disorder, a label the families received with roughly the enthusiasm you’d expect.

I’ve delivered that diagnosis myself. The MRI was perfect, the legs still wouldn’t move, and the patient heard “it’s all in your head” no matter how carefully I phrased it. She left to find a doctor who would order another scan.

A toxin is a gift, because it blames no one. A functional diagnosis blames no one either, yet patients hear an accusation in it, and plenty of us deliver it like one. We fumble that conversation more often than we fumble a central line.

Among the Miskito people on Nicaragua’s Caribbean coast, young women fall prey to grisi siknis. They collapse, then bolt into the night, and later describe a dark stranger who came to carry them off.

Wealthy countries have their own spirits. In El Carmen de Bolívar, Colombia, in 2014, schoolgirls began fainting and convulsing after HPV vaccination. Videos of their episodes ricocheted across social media, and the country’s HPV vaccination rate collapsed.

Two years later, American diplomats in Havana reported headaches, dizziness and strange sounds, and the press settled on a mysterious energy weapon. Some neurologists argue for a more mundane explanation that nobody in Washington wanted to hear.

Our culture supplies the toxins, the radio waves and the MRI that might at last catch the culprit. The Miskito get a dark stranger, while our demons come with CPT codes.

Funerals are where the haunted house collides with your financial plan. The National Funeral Directors Association put the 2023 median cost of a funeral with viewing and burial at about $8,300, and a funeral with cremation at roughly $6,280. Your aunt’s flower budget comes extra.

Whole-body donation to a medical school typically covers transport and cremation and returns the ashes to family, often at little or no cost. Programs vary, so call the school before you count on it.

Your body could spend its retirement crash-testing airbags or showing some nervous first-year where the brachial plexus hides. Mine would be in good company. I still owe that woman with the coral nail polish.

Physicians spend years making sure the 401(k) has a beneficiary. Few of us spend ten minutes deciding who gets the rest of the estate, meaning the part with the liver in it. Put it in writing this Halloween, somewhere between the will and the trust, and let your remains keep earning after you clock out.

#8543. JAL Business Class via Multiple Transfer Partners

World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings

Picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific. The door closes. A flight attendant in a crisp JAL uniform offers you a warm towel and asks how you'd like your appetizer served. The flat bed is already made with a proper duvet. Outside the window, the sun is setting over the ocean. You're nine hours into a 12-hour flight to Tokyo, and you feel more rested than you did when you boarded. This is JAL's Sky Suite — one of the most celebrated business class products in the world — and with the right travel rewards strategy, your family can experience it for a fraction of what everyone else is paying. Here's the math that stops people cold: a round-trip business class ticket from San Francisco to Tokyo on JAL typically retails for **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's not a typo. Premium transcontinental fares are genuinely that expensive, and most people simply accept that they'll never sit up front on a 12-hour flight across the Pacific. But the ChooseFI community knows better. That same seat — the same flat bed, the same Champagne, the same Sky Suite cocoon — is available for **60,000 miles** when booked through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. At a retail value of $5,000 to $10,000, you're looking at **8.3 to 16.7 cents per point** in value. For context, most travel rewards experts consider anything above 1.5 cents per point a good redemption. This one can be up to *eleven times* that benchmark. The pricing inefficiency exists because partner award programs — like Alaska and American — use fixed award charts that were negotiated years ago, before JAL's hard product became one of the most sought-after cabins in the sky. JAL hasn't raised these partner pricing levels proportionally as cash fares have climbed. The gap between what you pay in points and what the market charges in dollars is enormous, and it's yours to exploit right now. This isn't a loophole that's about to close tomorrow. It's a structural feature of the loyalty system — one that rewards people who understand how to use their points strategically rather than burning them on domestic economy upgrades. For anyone on the path to financial independence, where every dollar and every point is treated with intention, this is exactly the kind of asymmetric opportunity worth understanding.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award. This is the aha moment that separates casual points users from strategic ones.

JAL operates its own loyalty program — JAL Mileage Bank — but it charges significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often running $100 to $500 or more per ticket. When you book JAL business class through JAL Mileage Bank itself, those surcharges erode a substantial portion of your points value before you even leave the ground. The ChooseFI community's editorial guidance here is unambiguous: book JAL through partner programs to avoid this tax on your redemption.

There are two primary programs where you can book JAL business class at 60,000 miles round-trip on the transpacific route:

Alaska Mileage Plan prices JAL business class at 60,000 miles for a round-trip between North America and Japan. Alaska is a oneworld partner of JAL and honors JAL's genuinely strong award availability. Critically, Alaska does not pass through JAL's fuel surcharges to awards booked through Mileage Plan. This is a massive advantage.

American AAdvantage also prices the same route at 60,000 miles round-trip. Both programs use fixed award charts, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash fares do — a $10,000 ticket at peak cherry blossom season costs exactly the same points as a ticket in a slower travel month.

Neither Alaska Mileage Plan nor American AAdvantage is a direct transfer partner from the major US bank programs in the same way Chase or Amex partners work. However, you have real pathways:

For Alaska and American miles specifically, the strongest earning strategies involve:

Both Alaska and American use fixed award charts — meaning the price in miles is the same regardless of how high the cash price climbs. This is the structural inefficiency at work. A seat that retails for $10,000 during peak season still costs 60,000 miles. The chart doesn't care about demand; it just prices by region and cabin. As long as JAL releases availability — and they do — the gap between cash cost and points cost remains enormous.

JAL also allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award, which means you can potentially add a stop in Tokyo itself while continuing to another Japanese city, or fly into one city and out of another — all at no additional miles cost.

This is the cardinal rule of all travel rewards bookings: never transfer points until you have confirmed availability. Points transfers are generally irreversible.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) to search for JAL award availability. Because BA is also a oneworld partner, their search tool shows you JAL award space. Search for your route (e.g., SFO to NRT) in business class. Any availability you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well. Look for "J" class availability, which represents business class award space.

You can also call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522 or American Airlines at 1-800-433-7300 and ask their agents to search JAL availability on your dates. Agents sometimes see space that doesn't show up online.

JAL's booking window opens 360 days in advance. For peak travel periods — Golden Week in Japan (late April to early May), cherry blossom season (late March to early April), and the summer holidays — availability disappears fast. Set a calendar reminder to search and book as soon as the window opens for your target dates.

For travel year-round outside those peaks, JAL is known for releasing strong business class availability, which is why this sweet spot earns a 4/5 on availability. You have real flexibility here.

Decide whether you'll book through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. Both charge 60,000 miles round-trip. The key differentiator: Alaska does not pass through fuel surcharges. If minimizing out-of-pocket costs is your priority, Alaska is the better choice.

For Alaska miles: Apply for the Bank of America Alaska Airlines Visa, earn the welcome bonus, and use shopping portals and partner promotions to top up. For American miles: The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select or Barclays AAdvantage Aviator cards offer solid welcome bonuses. You'll need a minimum of 60,000 miles per person.

If you need to use the Capital One → JAL Mileage Bank transfer path, initiate the transfer from your Capital One portal. Transfers post in 1-2 days. Note that booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly will incur fuel surcharges.

For Alaska: Call 1-800-252-7522 or book online at alaskaair.com/partner-awards. Online booking of JAL awards through Alaska can be hit-or-miss; calling is often more reliable.

For American: Book at aa.com or call. American's website allows partner award searches, though calling often surfaces additional availability.

Once booked, confirm your ticket number, that the cabin shows as "Business" (not an upgrade), and request your preferred meal. JAL offers Western and Japanese meal options — request ahead. Your seat assignment on the 787-9 Sky Suite or 777-300ER Apex Suite can be made at booking.

The core arbitrage here is the difference between booking through JAL's own program versus booking through oneworld partner programs. JAL Mileage Bank imposes significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets — often $100 to $500 per ticket — which erodes the points value substantially. But Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage can book the exact same JAL-operated flights with zero fuel surcharges because they use their own award charts and pricing rules. You are flying on JAL's aircraft with JAL's crew and JAL's business class product, but paying through a partner program's more favorable pricing. This is the same structural mismatch that creates sweet spots throughout the oneworld alliance — the booking program's pricing does not match the operating airline's product quality.

Let's run the numbers on a specific scenario that thousands of ChooseFI members have used as a benchmark: San Francisco (SFO) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) in JAL business class, round-trip for two people.

A quick search on Google Flights or JAL's own website for this route in business class will typically show cash prices ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 per person — let's use $7,000 as a reasonable midpoint for this example. For two people, you're looking at a $14,000 cash outlay before you even think about hotels in Tokyo.

Booked through Alaska Mileage Plan: 60,000 Alaska miles per person, round-trip. For two travelers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles total, plus taxes and fees (which Alaska keeps minimal for JAL awards, typically under $100 for the pair).

The CPP math: $7,000 in value ÷ 60,000 miles = 11.7 cents per point — squarely in the middle of the 8.3-to-16.7-cent range and nearly 8 times what most people get burning points on domestic economy tickets.

On the 777-300ER, you may get the Apex Suite — a staggered configuration with direct aisle access from every seat and a similarly flat, private sleeping environment.

Beyond the hardware: JAL's service is routinely ranked among the best in the world. The meal service for a 12-hour transpacific flight is multi-course, the sake selection is curated, and the attention to detail in Japanese hospitality culture elevates the experience above what the points price alone suggests.

You'll also access the JAL First Class Lounge or JAL Business Class Lounge at Narita on the return — another perk included with your business class boarding pass. By the time you land in San Francisco after a flat-bed sleep and a proper breakfast service, you've experienced what most travelers save for a once-in-a-lifetime trip. With travel rewards, it can be your default way to cross the Pacific.

British Airways' award search at ba.com is one of the best tools for seeing oneworld partner availability without committing any miles. Use it to scout JAL space across multiple dates before you transfer a single point. It shows business class availability clearly and quickly.

JAL's award calendar opens 360 days in advance. For anyone targeting cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or Golden Week (late April to early May), you should be searching and booking at the 360-day mark, not 60 days out. These are the hardest windows to find availability. Outside peak Japan travel seasons, this is much more forgiving.

JAL Mileage Bank allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award. If you're booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly (accepting the fuel surcharges), you can fly into Tokyo and out of Osaka, for example, without additional miles. This is a genuine value-add for anyone planning a broader Japan itinerary — no backtracking required.

This is a small thing that makes a big difference. Request the Japanese meal option when booking. It's more authentic, better-suited to the overall experience, and — in the ChooseFI spirit of intentionality — it's why you chose this airline over a generic carrier.

This is the single most common and most painful mistake. Points transfers are almost always one-way and irreversible. Never, under any circumstances, transfer points to a program before you have verbal or written confirmation of the award space you intend to book.

As emphasized in the program overview: JAL charges significant fuel surcharges on awards booked through its own program — $100 to $500 or more. For transpacific routes, always book through Alaska or American to avoid these fees. The data is explicit on this point.

If you do earn JAL Mileage Bank miles directly, note that they expire 36 months from the date earned on a rolling basis. If you let a balance sit idle, you may lose miles before you've accumulated enough to book. Keep the balance active through small purchases or partner activity.

This sweet spot is best suited for couples and individual travelers who are targeting Japan specifically — whether it's a bucket-list trip, a first visit to Tokyo, or a multi-city Japan itinerary. The fixed 60,000-mile price per person means that families with young children will need to accumulate significant balances (60,000 miles per ticketed passenger), which pushes the complexity and earning requirement higher.

You need a minimum of 60,000 Alaska miles or 60,000 American AAdvantage miles per person to execute this redemption. For a couple, that's 120,000 miles — achievable with two well-chosen credit card welcome bonuses plus some additional earning through everyday spending or partner promotions.

This redemption is not ideal for beginners — it scores 2/5 on beginner-friendliness, and honestly, that's accurate. The booking path involves navigating partner award searches, understanding the difference between booking programs (Alaska vs. JAL Mileage Bank) and why it matters for surcharges, and potentially calling airlines rather than booking online. If you're on your first or second travel rewards card and still building your foundational understanding, this is one to put on a future list while you sharpen your skills.

For the FI-focused traveler who has been in the travel rewards ecosystem for a year or more, this is a landmark redemption. The CPP ceiling of 16.7 cents per point represents one of the highest-value uses of any points in a North American loyalty portfolio. If you believe in maximizing every dollar you earn and every point you accumulate — and the ChooseFI community does — this is the kind of redemption that justifies the entire system.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty**, and that rating is honest. It's not the most complex thing in the travel rewards world, but it has enough moving parts that going in without preparation can lead to frustration or costly mistakes. **What specifically makes it moderate:** First, the **earning path is not plug-and-play**. Unlike Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, which transfer to dozens of partners instantly, Alaska miles and American miles are earned primarily through co-branded credit cards and flying. There's no one magic transferable currency that flows directly into these programs at full value. Second, **the booking process often requires a phone call**. Online partner award booking through Alaska and American works inconsistently. Many experienced travelers report that calling the airline's award desk surfaces availability that the website doesn't show — which is a normal part of the process but adds friction. Third, **fuel surcharge awareness matters**. Understanding *why* you book through Alaska or American instead of JAL Mileage Bank directly is a non-obvious nuance that could cost you real money if you don't get it right. **Three tips to overcome the challenge:** 1. **Use BA.com as your availability scouting tool** — it gives you a clean, visual look at JAL award space without committing any miles. 2. **Call Alaska or American directly** when online searches fail. Agents are well-versed in partner award booking and can often find and hold space while you confirm your miles balance. 3. **Build your miles balance before you start searching.** Having 70,000+ miles in hand (a small buffer above 60,000) before you begin reduces stress and gives you flexibility on dates. If you've already completed one or two simpler travel rewards bookings and understand the basics of award searches, this is well within reach. The effort is real — and the payoff is a flat bed over the Pacific.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) and search for your route in business class. Because BA is a oneworld partner, their search tool shows JAL award space. Search across multiple dates to find availability. Any space you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well.

Both charge 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges. Alaska miles can be earned through the Alaska Airlines Visa card or transferred from Marriott Bonvoy (3:1). AAdvantage miles can be earned through Citi cards or transferred from various hotel programs. Choose based on which miles you have or can earn most efficiently.

Only transfer points after confirming award availability on ba.com. For Alaska, earn through card spending or Marriott transfers. For AAdvantage, earn through Citi cards. Never transfer before confirming space — transfers are generally irreversible.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan or book on aa.com to ticket the JAL-operated flight. For Alaska, phone booking is required for partner awards. For AA, search on aa.com and book online if the JAL space appears. Confirm your JAL seat assignment on jal.com after ticketing.

JAL Mileage Bank imposes fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often adding $100 to $500 per ticket on transpacific routes. Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage book the exact same JAL-operated flights at the same 60,000-mile price but with zero fuel surcharges. You fly the same plane, same seat, same service — but pay significantly less out of pocket.

JAL opens its award calendar approximately 360 days in advance. For peak seasons like cherry blossom season (late March to early April) and Golden Week (late April to early May), you should begin searching the day the window opens. Off-peak dates are generally easier to find with 3 to 6 months of lead time.

Not directly, but you can use Chase points indirectly. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards to British Airways Avios and book JAL through BA's oneworld partnership. However, BA charges fuel surcharges on partner awards, so this path is less favorable than Alaska or AA. The cleanest Chase path is to earn Alaska or AA miles through other means.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

JAL business class via Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage is the definitive sweet spot for anyone targeting Japan. At 60,000 miles one-way with zero fuel surcharges, you are booking a $5,000 to $10,000 cash experience for a fraction of the cost through a partner program pricing arbitrage. The key is searching ba.com for availability before transferring a single point, booking 360 days out for peak cherry blossom or Golden Week dates, and choosing between Alaska and AA based on which miles you can earn most efficiently. JAL's business class product — lie-flat seats, exceptional cuisine, and Japanese hospitality — delivers an experience that justifies the points spend and then some. This is the redemption that puts Japan within reach for every FI-minded traveler.

#8541. Should I Come Out of Retirement?

More than 60% of respondents in a 2026 Goldman Sachs survey of 5,106 working and retired Americans said they had taken work outside their primary job, most out of necessity rather than a wish for extra spending money. Nearly 70% had delayed a major financial goal.

Retirement is increasingly becoming a touchy topic for many, especially those of us who are used to a certain level of stability.

The news only makes matters worse. On Friday, October 30, we saw Nasdaq’s biggest 1-day drop since June 5, setting the internet ablaze with speculation. The index closed 7.8% below its October 6 record, though it was noted that the S&P 500 was only a few percent below its own record.

Then there’s inflation. Annual inflation reached 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August. Pair that with continuing international conflicts on several fronts, and you’ve got the perfect storm of insecurity.

A National Institute on Retirement Security survey found that 80% of Americans say that the nation faces a retirement crisis and 61% worry they won’t be financially secure in retirement.

The respondents blamed inflation (73%) and market volatility (62%) as contributing factors, and 76% feared Social Security cuts if Congress fails to act.

A New York Life survey of more than 2,000 adults found that 34% had already delayed retirement or planned to, and 46% of them expected to push it back 5 years or more. Their top reasons were a lack of savings (46%) and inflation (45%).

Those who have already retired aren’t immune to these insecurities. The Goldman Sachs sample included 1,494 retirees aged 45 to 75. A market drop may also hurt more when you’re drawing from a portfolio than when you’re adding to it.

So, wondering if you should go back to work feels like a warranted question. Plenty of retirees take the leap back. Doctors go back too, though plenty of them say they don’t miss it. In a recent r/emergencymedicine thread, retired ED physicians were split on the question.

One, 3 years out, said he doesn’t miss it at all and still has the occasional nightmare. Another quit at 61 with no plan, misses the people and belonging to the group and keeps looking for work without luck.

1.5 million retirees reentered the workforce by March 2022.

We spend decades planning for the day we stop working. Then some of us stop, and a year or 2 later we’re checking job boards or answering calls from our old group. If that sounds like you, this article is for you.

Let’s take a look at the reasons many doctors feel the urge to un-retire, what going back to work in 2026 entails and the logistics of it all.

In case you missed it: Micro-retirements aren’t a shortcut to FIRE

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Money is the top reason many retirees choose to go back, so let’s start there. A recent survey found that 48% of working retirees said they needed the income, while 45% said they worked for social and emotional benefits.

Divide 1 year of spending by your portfolio. An example in T. Rowe Price’s example illustrates a 62-year-old with $900,000 who spends $65,000 a year.

That’s a 7.2% withdrawal rate. She has a 64% chance of not outliving her money if she retires at 62, a 91% chance at 65 and a 97% chance at 67.

Now let’s imagine a physician-specific version.

Say you have $2,500,000 and spend $150,000 a year before taxes. That’s a 6% withdrawal rate. A part-time job paying $60,000 would trim your withdrawals to $90,000, which is 3.6%.

You lower your rate by 2.4 percentage points without changing how you live. Of course, taxes will reduce that paycheck so ask your planner for a clearer outline.

One retired doctor said he saved about 30% of his take-home pay in his last years of full-time work, and his spending ended up around half of his colleagues’.

He could walk away any day, and his group knew it. That kind of freedom is helpful even after you return because you’re able to negotiate better when you don’t actually need the job.

Before you take a job, figure out whether the problem is your portfolio or your spending. If your withdrawal rate looks fine but spending still makes you uneasy, a concrete spending plan may help more than a paycheck. Ask your planner to set a monthly amount you can spend without second-guessing.

Working longer also helps in 2 other ways. You can delay account withdrawals as well as Social Security. Benefits grow 8% for every year you wait past full retirement age until you reach 70, while claiming at 62 cuts them by almost 30%.

Continuing to work also gives you more time to contribute to your retirement accounts. If your new employer offers a 401(k) or 403(b), the 2026 limit is $24,500, plus an $8,000 catch-up at 50 and older or $11,250 at ages 60 to 63.

It depends on whether you’ve claimed it and how old you are. If you haven’t claimed, going back to work is straightforward and your eventual monthly SS check will continue to increase.

If you claimed before full retirement age (FRA), the earnings test applies. In 2026, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 if you’re under FRA all year.

In the year you reach FRA, the limit rises to $65,160, and the agency withholds $1 for every $3 above it. Only earnings before the month you reach FRA count.

If your part-time schedule pays more than $24,480, expect withholding. The money isn’t gone for good, though. Social Security recalculates your benefit at FRA to credit the months it withheld.

Only wages and self-employment earnings count, so investment income doesn’t trigger withholding. Once you reach FRA, working doesn’t reduce your benefit.

You’ll also keep paying Social Security taxes on your paychecks. Higher earnings can also make more of your benefit taxable, so ask your tax preparer to estimate that too.

What if you changed your mind after claiming early? If you claimed before FRA, you have 12 months to withdraw your application. You must repay what you received, and Social Security then treats your record as if you never claimed at all.

Coverage before 65 costs far more in 2026 than it did in 2025 since the enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025.

KFF reports that a 60-year-old with a $65,000 income now pays an average of $10,389 more per year, or $865 per month. The subsidy cliff is also back which means above 400% of the poverty level (which is $62,600 for a single person in 2026), you lose the premium tax credit entirely.

On top of that, the ACA allows insurers to charge adults in their 60s up to 3 times what they charge adults in their 20s.

So a job with group health coverage may save you thousands of dollars a year because it skips the marketplace and the income cliff.

A working physician said that if he left medicine early, he’d take a flexible management job of about 25 hours a week mostly for the group insurance and the 401(k) match.

If you’re considering the same, ask HR what hours are required for benefits and when coverage starts, since each plan sets its own cutoff.

Medicare changes much of the picture. If you delayed Part B because you had coverage through your own or your spouse’s current job, you get an 8-month special enrollment period after that job or coverage ends.

If you miss it, you’ll have to pay 10% more for each full 12-month period you could have had Part B, for as long as you keep it. COBRA and retiree coverage don’t count for that exemption.

Keep in mind that Medicare generally pays first if the employer has fewer than 20 employees. So a small practice’s plan may pay second and you’d still need Part B.

Learn more: 11 Retirement Planning Mistakes That Haunt High-Earning Physicians

Don’t count on getting your old job back.

An AARP survey of more than 3,500 people ages 50 and older found that 74% believe their age will be a barrier to getting hired, and 64% of workers 50 and older have seen or experienced age discrimination at work. That stigma is even worse for women.

Another AARP report found that 37% of workers 50 and older experienced subtle age discrimination during a job search in 2025, up from 30% in 2024. These surveys cover all fields, not only medicine, so ask recruiters in your specialty what they are seeing firsthand.

Think about what you want the next job to be. 24% of workers 50 and older planned a job change in 2025, so you won’t be the only one looking. If your retirement was driven mostly due to clinical work, teaching, consulting or chart review may suit you better than your old schedule.

We’ve already established that money drives about half of all unretirements. Boredom and a wish to help others drive many of the rest.

In an AARP survey, 18% of unretirees said boredom or a desire to stay active was their main reason for returning to work. For doctors, these sentiments start even before they leave.

In a Jackson Physician Search survey, 44% of physicians feared losing their sense of purpose in retirement and 39% feared boredom (money was still the top fear at 53%).

In CHG Healthcare’s 2024 survey, physicians who wanted to keep working felt that way because of a love of medicine (58%), social connections (57%) and concern for patients (39%). Others stated not feeling emotionally ready (47%), wanting to keep their lifestyle (35%) and fearing boredom or isolation (33%).

In Medscape’s 2025 retirement report, the top reason physicians gave for not retiring earlier was feeling they still had more to offer (62%), ahead of not having enough saved (45%). In the 2023 report, 46% expected retirement to feel like losing a part of their identity.

Retired and soon-to-retire ED physicians on Reddit offer a mixed bag of insights. One commenter who was 4 months from retiring expects to miss the ego boost of being a doctor. The one who quit at 61 with no plan misses colleagues and most of his patients, though not the fatigue of rotating shifts or the dread of sending home someone who should have stayed. Several said sleep and a normal daytime rhythm were the biggest change.

Retirement also changes what stresses you out. A 2025 Mayo Clinic review of physician well-being in retirement says that stress moves from work problems to personal ones, including professional identity, family, health and the loss of relationships.

The journal’s late-career paper urges physicians to plan for social and emotional needs along with finances. If you can’t picture your days without the work and the people, look at part-time options before you retire fully.

Give your first year in retirement a fair shake before you decide. People who leave long, consuming careers often describe a rocky start to retirement.

One user on Reddit said that it took about a year to stop feeling guilty about doing nothing. Another lasted 2 years, took a part-time job and has stayed 10 years. A third said the new job mattered to them mostly for the community, since all their friends still worked.

In case you missed it: The Nightmare Before Retirement: A Physician’s Cautionary Tale (2026 Edition)

If burnout pushed you out in the first place, the same job will push you out again. In 2026, burnout in healthcare is still running rampant.

Doximity’s May 2026 poll found that 82% of physicians say they’re overworked and 46% are considering early retirement because of it.

That number is up from 37% in 2025 and 21% in 2021. The jump is sharpest among women (54% in 2026 compared to 33% in 2023) and physicians ages 50 to 54 (56%, up from 35%).

Medscape’s 2026 burnout report corroborates this. 50% of male and 51% of female physicians say that their work causes their burnout, and 13%–14% are considering leaving medicine altogether.

In a MedCentral survey, 44% of physicians said they had considered leaving medical practice since the start of the year.
